"Oh, yes. I saw it officially announced in this morning's papers. And, by-the-by, lam very much afraid he is to take command of our regimer..t, and be my superior officer." '-Oh, Herbert, I hope and pray not! I think there is wickedness enough packed up in that man's body to si4 a squadron or lose an army I' "Well,* Cap, such things will happen. Atten- tion! There's Sauter ready to call his witnesses." And, in truth, the next moment Capitola Black was called to the stand. . _ _

Cap took her place and gave her evidence con amore, and with such vim and such expressions of indignation, that Stringfellow reminded her she was there to give testimony, and not to plead the cause. Cap rejoined that she was perfectly willing to do both 1 And so she continued not only to tell the facts, but to express her opinions as to the motives of Le Noir, and gave her judgment as to what should be the decision of the court.

Stringfellow, the attorney for Colonel Le Noir, I evidently thought that in this rash, reckless, spirited witness, he had a. fine subject for sarcastic cross-examination! But he reckoned "without his host." He did not knew Cap I He too, "caught a Tartar." And before the cross-examination was concluded, Capitola.'s apt and cutting replies had overwhelmed him with ridicule and confusion, and. done more for the cause of her friend than all her . partisans put together! Other witnesses were called to corroborate the testimony of Capitola, and still others were examined to prove the last expressed wishes of the late William Day, in regard to the disposal of his daughter's person during the period of her mino- rity. There was no effective rebutting evidence, and after some hard arguing on bothsides, the case was closed, and the judge deferred his decision until the third day thereafter. The parties then left the oourt and returned to their several lodgings. Old Hurricane gave no one a civil word that day. Wool was an atrocious villain, an incendiary scoundrel, a cut-throat and a black demon Cap was a beggar, a vagabond, and a vixen. Herbert Greyson was another beggar, besides reing a knave, a fop, and an impudent puppy. The inn-keeper was a swindler, the waiters thieves, the whole world was going to ruin, where it well deserved to go, and all mankind to the demon—as he hoped and trusted they would ! And all this tornado of passion and invective arose just because he had unexpectedly met in the court-room the patient face and beseeching eyes of a woman, married and forsaken, loved and lost, long ago! Was it strange that Herbert, who had so re- sented his treatment of Marah Rocke, should bear all his fury, injustice and abuse- of himself and others with such compassionwe forbearance? But he not only forbore to resent his own affronts, but also besought Capitola to have patience with the old man's temper, and apologised to the host, by saying that Major Warfield had been very severely tried that day, and when calmer, would be the first to regret the violence of his own words. Marah Rocke returned with Clara to the old doctor's house. She was more patient, silent and quiet than before. Her face was a little paler, her eyes softer, and her tones lower—that was the' only visible effect of the morning's unexpected rencontre. The next day but one all the parties concerned assembled at the court-house to hear the decision of the judge. It was given as had been anticipated in the favour of Clara Day, who was permitted in accordance with her father's approved wishes, to reside in her patrimonial home, under the care of Mrs. Marah Rocke. Colonel Le Noir was to re- main trustee of the property, with directions from the court immediately to pay the legacies left by the late Doetor Day to Marah Rocke and Traverse Rocke, and also to pay to Clara Day, in quarterly instalments, from the revenue of her property, an annual slim or money, sufficient for her support. This dec43ion tilled the hearts -of Clarah and her friends with joy. Forgetting time.and place, she threw herself into the arms of .Marah ,Rocke and wept with delight. All concerned in the trial then sought their loadings. Clara and Mrs. Rocks returned to the cottage to make 'preparation.s for removing to Willow Heights. Doctor Williams went to the agent of the pro- perty to require him to give up the keys, which he. did without hesitation. Old hurricane and his party packed up, to .be ready for the :.-tage to tjte., them to Tip Top they next day. But that night a series of mysterious events were • . said .to have taken ri:ace, at the deserted house at Willow -heights, that tilled vac whole community with superstitious wonder. It was reported by numbers of gad' criers and farmers, who passed that yoad on their way to early, market, that a perfect witches' sabbath had been held in that empty house all night.! That lights had appeared flitting from ro---rn to room; that stramgc weir& faces had looked out from rho windows ; and wild .. screams had pierced the air! The next day when this report had reached the ears of Clara, and she was asked by-Doctor Wil- liams whether she would not be afraid to live :there, she laughed gaily and bade him try her. Cap who had come over to take leave of Clara, joined her in her merriment., declared that she, for her part, doted on ghosts, and that after Herbert Greyson's depart ore, she should come and visit Clara and' help her to entertain the spectres. Clara replied that she -should hold her to her promise. And so the friends kissed and separated. That same day saw several removals. , Clara and Mrs. Rocke took up their abode At Willow Heights, and seized an hour even of that busy time, to write to Traverse and apprise him of their good fortune. Old Hurrioane and his party set out for their home, where they arrived before nightfall. . And the next day but one Herbert Greyson took leave of his friends and departed to join his eons. golly on their road to glory.
CHAPTER XLIII. BLACK DONALD.
" Feared, shunned, belied ere youth had lost her force, He hated men too much to feel remorse,
And thought the vice of wrath a sacred call, To pay the injuries of some on all.
" There was a laughing devil in his sneer, That caused emotions both of rage and. fear; And where his frown of hatred darkly fell, Hope, withering; fled, and mercy sighed farewell V". —BYRON.

Herbert Greyson had been correct in his con- jecture concerning the cause of Colonel Le Noir's conduct in absenting himself from the. trial, or ap- pearing there .nly in the person of his attorney. A proud, vain, conceited man, full of Joseph Surfaceism, he coald better have borne to be arraigned upon the charge of murder than to face the accusation of baseness that was about to be proved upon him. Being reasonably certain as to what was likely to be the .iecision of the Orphans' Court, he was not disappointed in bearing that judgment had been rendered in favour of is ward and her friends. His one great disappointment had been upon diseoverinc, the flight of Clara. For when he had ascertained that she had fled, he knew that all was lost—and lost through Capitola —the hated girl for whose destruction he had now another and a stronger motive—revenge. In this mood of mind, three days before his de- p +rture to join his regiment, he sought the retreat of the outlaw. He chose an early hour of the even- ing as that in which he should be most likely to find Black Donald. It was about eiJit o'clock when he wrapped his large cloak around his tall figure, pulled .his hat low over his sinister brows, and set out to walk alone to the secret cavern in the side of the Demon s Punoh Bowl. _ _

- The night was dark and the path dangerous ; but his directions had been careful, so that when he r ached the brink of that awful abyss, he knew precisely where to begin his descent with the least danger of being precipitated to the bottom. And by taking a strong hold upon the stunted saplings of pine and cedar that grew down through the clefts or the ravine, and niacin; his feet firmly upon the points of projecting rocks, he contrived to descend the inside of that horrible abystn, which from the top seemed to be fraught with cer- tain death to any one daring enough to make the attempt. When about half way down the precipice he reached the clump of cedar bushes growing in the deep cleft, and concealing the hole that forme4 the entrance to the cavern. _

Here he paused, and looking through the entrance into a dark and apparently fathomless cavern, he gave the peculiar signal whistle, which was immediately answered from within by the well-kown voice of the outlaw chief, saying: "All right, my Colonel. Give us your hand. Be careful now; the floor of this cavern is several feet below the opening." Le Noir extended his hand into the darkness within and soon felt it grasped by that of Black Donalda_whoonattprinsj !!dwly, my Cel- tic' !" succeeded in guiding biu down the utter

darkness of the subterranean descent until they upon iie firm bottom of the cavern. They were still in the midst of a blackness that might be felt, except that from a small opening in the side of the rock a light gleamed. Toward this second opening Black D. nald conducted his patron And stooping and passing before him, led him into an inner cavern, well lighted and rudely fitted up. Upon a large natural platform of rock, occu- pying the centre of the space, were some dozen bottles of brandy or whiskey, several loaves of bread, and some dried venison. Around this rude table, seated upon fragments of rock, lugged thither for the purpose, were some eight or ten men of the band, in various stages of intoxication. Along the walls were piles of be rskins, some of which served as couches for six or seven men, who had thrown themselves down upon them in a state of exhaus- tion or drunken stup,r. "Come, boys, we have not a boundless choice of apartments here, and I want to talk to my Col- onel. Suppose you take your liquor and bread and meat into the outer cavern, and give us the use of this for an hour," said the outlaw. The men sullenly obeyed and began to gather up the viands. Demon Dick seiz_d one of the lights !o go after them. "Put down toe glim. Satan singe your skin for you! Do you want to bring a hue and cry upon us ?7,7lYon't you know a light in the outer cavern can be seen from the outside ?" roared Black Donald. Dick sulkily set down the candle and followed his comrades. "What are you glummerinv, about? confound you! * You can see to eat and drink well enough and find your way to your mouth in the dark, you brute 1" thundered the captain. But as toere was no answer to this, and the men had retreated and left their chief with his vis'tor alone, Black Donald turned to Colonel La Noir, and said : _ _

"Well, my patron, what great matter is it that has caused you to leave the company of fair Clara Day for our grim society ?" "Al), then it appears you are not aware that Clara Day has fled from us! has made a successful appeal to the Orphans' Court, and been taken out of our hands?" angrily replied Colonel Le Noir. " Whe-cw I My Colonel, I think I could have managed that better. I think if I had had that girl in my power as you had, she should not have escaped me !" " Bah ! bah ! bah ! stop boasting since it was through your neglect —yours I yours ;—that I lost this girl." " Mine! " exclaimed Black Donald, in astonish- ment.

"Aye, yours! for if you had done your duty, performed your engagement, kept your word, and delivered roe from this fatal Capitola,' I had not lost my ward, nor my son his wealthy bride l" ex- claimed Le Noir, angrily. " Capitola ! Capitola again! What on earth had she to do with the loss of Clara Day ?" cried Black Donald in wonder.

"Everything to do with it, sir ! D./ a cunning artifice she delivered Clara from our power ; actually- set her free and covered her flight until she was in security I " "That girl again ! Ha-ha-ha-ha ha ! Ho-ho- ho-ho-ho !" laughed and roared Black Donald, slapping his knees. Le Noir ground and gnashed his teeth in rage, muttering hoarsely : " Yes I'you may laugh, confound you, since it is granted those who win to do so ! you may laugh ! for you have lone me out of five thousand dollars, and what on earth have you performed to earn it ?" "Come, &erne, my Colonel; fair and easy I don't know which is vulgarest, to betray loss of temper or love of money, and you are doing both I However, it is between frinids 1 But how the demon did that girl, that capital Capitola, get Clara off from right under your eyes ?" " By changing clothes with her! confound you ! I will tell you all about it," replied Le Noir, who thereupon commenced and related the whole stra- tagem by which Capitola freed Clara, incl,ding the manner in which she accompanied them to the church and revealed herself at the altar. Black Donald threw himself back and roared with laughter, vigorously slapping his knees, and crying: " That girl! that capital Capitola ? I would not sell my prospect of possessing her for double your bride
"Your prospect !' Your prospect is about as deceptive as a Wet morgana ! What have you been doing, I ask you again, towards realising this prospect, and earning the money you have already received ?"

"Fair and easy, my Colonel! Don't let temper get the better of justice What have I been doing , towards earning the money you have already paid inc I—ln the first place I lost my time and risked my liberty watching around Hurricane Hall. Then, when I had identified the girl and the room she slept in, by seeing her at her window, I put three of my best men in jeopardy to catch her! Then, when she, the witch; had captured them, I sacrificed all my good looks, transincgrifying my- self into a frightful old field preacher, and went to the camp-meeting to watch, among Other things, for an opportunity of carrying her off! The sorceress I--she gave me no such opportunity! I succeeded in nothing except in fooliir4 the wise- acres and getting admitted to the prison of my comrades, whom -I furnished with instruments by which they made their escape. Since that time we have had to lie low—yes literally—to lie low-- to keep out of sight, to burrow under ground! in a word, lo live-in this cavern !" " And since which you have abandoned all in- intention of getting the girl and earning the five thousand dollars," sneered Le Noir. "Earning the remaining five thousand, you mean. Colonel! The first five thousand I consider I have already earned. It was the last five thou- sand that I was to get when the girl should he disposed of." "Well ?" "Well, I have not given up, either the inten- tion of earning the money, or the hope of getting the girl ; in truth, I had rather lose the money than the girl. have been on the watch almost continually; but though I suppose she rides out frequently, I have not yet happened to hit upOn her in any of her excursions. At last, however, I have fixed upon a plan foi getting the 'witch into my power. I shall trust the execution of that plan to no one but Inset' I But I must have time." " Time ! perdition, sir! delay in this matter is fraught with danger! Listen, sir! How Warfield got possession of this girl, or the knowledge of her history I do not know, except that it was through the agency of that accursed hag, Nancy Grewell I —but that he has her, and that he knows all about her, is but too certain! That he has net at present legal proof enough to establish her identity and her rights before a court of justice, I infer from the fact of his continuing inactive in the matter. But who can foresee how soon he may obtain all the proof that is necessary to establish Capitola's claims, and wrest the whole of this property from me? Who can tell whether he is not now secretly engaged in seeking and collecting such proof ! therefore, I repeat, that the girl must immediately be got rid of —Donald! rid me of that creature and the day that you prove to me her death I will double your fee 1" "Agreed, my Colonel, agreed. I have no ob- jection to your do a bang, or even quatirupling my fee! you shall find me in that_tts in all other matters, perfectly amenable to reason. Only I must have time. Haste would ruin us. I repeat that I have a plan by which I am certain to get the girl into my possession. A plan, the execution of which I will intrust to no other hands but my own. But I conclude as I began—l must have time !" "And how much time?" exclaimed Le Noir, again losing his patience. "Easy, my patron. That I cannot tell you. It is imprudent to make promises, especially to you, who will take nothing into consideration, when they cannot be kept," replied Black Donald, coolly. "But, sir, do you not know that I am ordered to Mexico, and must leave within three days !—I would see the end of this before I go 1" angrily ex- claimed Le Noir. "Softly, softly, my child the Colonel Slow and sure!' Fair and easy goes far in a day 1' " "In a word, will you do this business for me and do it promptly ?" "Surely, surely, my patron ! But I insist upon time !" "But I go to Mexico in three days 1" "All honor go with you, my Colonel! Who . would keep his friend from the path of glory ?" " Perdition, sir, you trifle with me!' "Perdition, certainly, Colonel. There I per- fectly agree with you; but the rest of your sen- tence is wrong; I don't trifle with you!" " What in the fiend's name do you mean ?" "Nothing in the name of any absent friend of ours! I mean simply that you may go to— Mexico." "And—my business—" --" Can be done just as well, perhaps better, without you! Recollect, if you please, my Col- cunt, when you were absent with i Harrison n the

A MIDSUMMER Dream of the Millennium—To be able to sit m a draught without catching cold. " Ricins have wings ;" but, unfortunately, they seldom use them except to travel in the wrong direction. DIPLOMACY consists first in presenting your ultimatum, and then seeing how of it you can get. Tuz man who never argues with "children, women, or fools" is not likely to have many arg,u-
. ntents.
HAPPY is the woman who cannot see •how her daughters are going to get as good husbands as she did.

A GREAT many people believe in being just before they are generous, and it takes them so 1 long to be just that they never get time to be generous. CHARLEY GOODLY: "I owe everything to my mother." Bobby Lender: "Please don't overlook the ten you owe me." SUE: Tell me, when you were in the army, were you cool in the hour of danger ?" He: " Cool ! I actually shivered !" ERRlNG.—Student (translating) : " And--er— then—er—er —er—went—er and —er." Profes- sor: "Don't laugh, gentlemen—to err is human." OLD ENGLISH.—First She: "How ridiculous men are! Here he has written me a letter com- paring my eyes to stars, my teeth to pearls, and swearing that the sun retires abashed from the brightness of my presence." Second She: "I don't call that foolish. I think it pretty sniart of him—giving you the kind of love talk that was in vogue when you were a girl." Mn. SAYLF.S : "Why, my dear—why are you crying?" Mrs. Sayles (with sobs) : "Oh, John, don't you remember my new crepon skirt I got at such a bargain last week for fifteen shillings ? " Mr. Sayles: " Yes ; what then ? " Mrs. Sayles (weeping afresh) : "I p-p-passed Lacey's t-t-to- day, and they were all m-m-marked down to fourteen shillings and ninepenee. 800-hoo !" THEORY AND PRACTICE.—Mrs. Dorcas: "Our league of emancipated women is going to have a lecture on the social equality of the sex. You must be sure to come." Mrs. Cobwigger : "Certainly, my dear. I shall bring Miss Smith with me, as she believes in social equality." Mrs. Dorcas: "Not for the world. You know she isn't in our set." SHE: "Before we were married you said it would give you the greatest pleasure to gratify my every wish." He: "My dear, I said your lightest wish; and ru do it, too.' Two VICES.—" Smoking is a bad thing," said Wagg. "Look at Vesuvius—smoking all the time, and a constant source of danger." "True," said Jocose; "and allied,to its smoking, Vesuvius is always indulging in what the Irishman called a wee bit of th' crater.'" YOUNGLOVE : "May, dear, the bank cashier in- forms me that you have overdrawn your account?" ` Mrs. Younglove ? "He does! The villain! George, see here! There, now—only five cheques used, and my book nearly full! The miserable, dishonest scoundrel?" "You have brought new sunshine into my life," he said, rapturously.. "Do you mean that?" she asked, timidly. "Of course I mean it. Can you doubt me ? " "Oh, of course, I know you wouldn't intentionally misrepresent. But you know a young man so often thinks a girl has brought sunshine into his life when in reality it's. only moonshine." •- WITH EFFECT.—A temperance orator was hold- ing forth at the corner of a street in South London. 4` My friends," he cried, "let me warn you. As you value your lives, your wives and little ones, and your homes, do not drink such vile stuff as beer, or brandy, or whiskey. I say, 'no; but " Here he paused for effect. The audience burst into loud laughter—nor was the reason far to seek. The speaker had raised his arm in exhorta- tion, and his hand was now pointing to a placard -on an adjacent hoarding: This placard bore the words—" Drink only —'s Gin." It was a good advertisement for the gin, but it was not what the orator meant. • FAIR EXCHANGE.—The Japanese relate a story to their children of a certain nobleman, who, having eaten up his fortune, took rooms next door to a famous restaurant. in order that he might enjoy the odours of the cooking viands in the which he could no longer indulge himself. The proprietor, hearing of this, after some time presented a bill, wherein he charg ed- two yen fifty sen for the vapours of food inhaled by the poor nobleman during the month. Whereupon the ex-gourmet, calling for his old cash-box which now held but a few copper coins, shook it violently in the ears of the proprietor and replied—" As you charge me for the fumes of your food, I pay you with the sound of my money." WANTED THEM Bow - LEGGED. During last autumn a pitman was asked by a friend, who was very bow-legged, to purchase, when next " i' the toon," a pair of stockings for him. On the follow., ins pay Saturday the pitman entered the shop of a we'll-known hosier to . make the purchase. The shopman was most obliging, but hsving shown the intending purchaser, nearly every pair in stock, he at last, thought it time to ask of the man a more minute description of what was required. He said he had shown nearly all they had, and he was sure their shop was second to none, and as they had hitherto given satisfaction to all classes, it was strange that they could not now suit a cus- ,tomer. The pitman laconically replied—" What I want is a pair o' bow-legged yins.' IN THE DAYS OF -His YouTH.—On the anni- versary of American Independence in 1873 Lord Rosebery dmed at Lord Houghton's, among the • guests being the American Minister and Mr. J. L. Motley, the historian. Lord Rosebery was always _ youthful-looking, and, 20 years ago, seemed a mere boy. In the course of conversation, Lewd Houghton made some remarks on the occasion which had , brought them together. Motley, who . sat opposite Lord Rosebery, looking at him said— " Perhaps our young friend does not understand what we are talking about ? " He got for reply this—" Oh, don't I! . It's all about the bird of freedom and that sort of bunkum." What Mr. Motley thought of the precociousness and out- spokenness of the youth (he looked 16, but was was really 26) is not recorded. A BOY'S EFFORT To EXPLAIN THINGS:— " Mamma, do you like to kiss Mrs. Jewhillaker ? " "No, dear." "Do you think Mrs. Jewhillaker likes td kiss you?" "I don't think she does." "Then why do you and she always kiss when you meet?" "I don't know, dear." "Don't you think Mrs. Jewhillaker would rather you didn't kiss her ? " " I have no doubt of it." "Wouldn't you rather Mrs. Jewhillaker didn't kiss you?" "Oh, very much !'""Then that must be whys" HE SAW IT.—Old -J. B—, who is a bit of a miser, has a friend, who is a bit of a wag. 5 had occasion to call at B—'s residence to discuss a business matter. The affair took longer to settle than was anticipated; in fact, B—'s dinner-hour ceshe round, and still the negotiations remained unfinished, B--- could hardly help asking S to stay. He did so with ill-feigned cordiality. To his great horror, S promptly accepted the invitation. "It's very plain—Lvery plaip, indeed," said B , apologetically. " Never mind, .my dear . sir," returned 5--, " I'm not accustomed to dainties." Two small—exceedingly small—chops were put upon the table. " There, ' said B—, with a rueful smile, "you see your dinner." "Yes," said B—, cheerfully, forking them both on his plate; "but, I don't see youra ! " A LITTLE MISTAKE.—Not one hundred miles from Glasgow lives" an old lady who is very wealthy, very irascible, and also very fond of whisky. Recently the parish council elections were held, and she had been constantly worried by a certain candidate to poll her vote in his favour. The polling station at which she had to vote was a certain temperance institute. She promised her vote to the candidate and proceeded , one morning to the poll. She was shown into a room and provided with pen and ink, and was told to sign her name in a certain book. After doing so she looked up quite pleased, and asked if her candidate had any chance. of being returned. The man in charge, after much thought, saw she had made a•Mlitake, and told her that'the polling took place on the_ following day. Without a word, she bounced out of the room in a temper. P..—She had unwittingly signed the temperance pledge. •

div.p: THE HIDDEN HAND;
CAPITOLA THE MADCAP. BY MRS. E. D. E. N. BOUT 11 WORT H.
CHAPTER XLII.

OAP "RESTS ON HER LAURELS" AND "SPOILS FOR A FIGHT." "'Tis hardly in a body's power, To keep at times frae being sour, To see how things are shared; How best o' chiels are whiles in want, While coofs and countless thousands rant, And ken na how to wearl." —BURNS.

Leaving Clara Day and Marah Rocke in a home of safety, plenty and kindness in the old doctor's house, we must run down to Hurricane Hall, to see what mischief Cap has been getting into since we left her! In truth, none. Cap had had such a surfeit of adventures, that she was fain to lie by and rest upon her laurels. Besides, there seemed just now nothing to do—no tyrants to take down, no robbers to capture, no distressed damsels to deliver, and Cap was again in danger of "spoiling for a fight." And then Herbert Greyson was at the- Hall—Herbert Greyson whom she vowed always did make a Miss Nancy of her ! And so Cap had to content herself for a week with quiet mornings of needle-work at her work-stand, with Herbert to read to or talk with her; sober afternoon rides, attended by Herbert and Old Hurricane; and hum- drum evenings at the chessboard, with the same Herbert, while Major Warfield dozed ilia great "sleepy hollow" of an arm-chair. One afternoon when they were out riding through the woods beyond the Demon's Run, a sheriff's officer rode up, and bowing to the party, presented a suspicious-looking document to Capitola, and a similar one to Herbert Greyson. And while Old Hurrieane stared his eyes half out, the parties most interested opened the papers, which they found to be rather pressing invitations to be present at a certain solemnity at Staunton. In a word, they were subpoenaed to give testimony in the case of Williams v. Le Noir. Here's a dialolical dilemma !" said Old Hur- ricane to himself, as soon as he learned the pur- port, of these documents; here I shall have to bring Cap into Court face to face with that demon to bear witness against him. Suppose, losing one ward he should lay c aim to another! Ah, but he can't without foully criminating himself. Well, well, we shall see 1" While Old hurricane was cogitating, Cap was exulting. "Oh, won't I tell all I kriow 1 Yes, and more too!' she exclaimed, in triumph. " ' More too 1' oh! hoity-toity! never say more too !' said Herbert, laughing. "I will, for I'll tell all, I suspect 1" said Cap, galloping on ahead, in her eagerness to get home and pack up for her journey. The next day Old Hurricane, Herbert Greyson, Capitola, Pitapat and Wool went by stage to Staunton. They put up at the Planters' and Farmers' Hotel, whence Herbert Greyson and Cap- irola soon sallied forth to see Clara and Mrs. Rocke. They soon found the doctor. s house, and were ushered into the parlour in the presence of their friends, _

The meeting between Capitola and Clara, and between Mrs. Rocke and Herbert was very cordial. And then Herbert introduced Capitola to Mrs. Rocke,-and Cap presented Herbert to Clara. And they all entered into conversation upon the'subject of the coming lawsuit, and the circumstanees that led to it. And Clara and Capitola related to each other all that had happened to each after their ex- changing Clothes mad parting. And when they had laughed over their mutual adventures and misad- ventures, Herbert and Capitola took leave and returned to their hotel. t

Herbert Greyson was the. most serious of the whole family. Upon reaching the hotel he went to his own roongod fell into deep reflection. And this was the course of his thoughts: "Ira Wanfield and Marah Rocke are here in the same town ! brought hither upon the same errand! to-Morrow to meet in the same court-room And yet not either.of them suspects the presence of the other. Mrs.. Rocke does not know that in Cap- itola's uncle she will behold Major Warfleld ! He does not foresee that in Clara's matronly friend he will behold Marsh Rocke. And Le Noir, the cause of all their mi*y, will be present, also. What will be the effect of this unexpected meeting? Ought I not to . warn one or the -other ?—Let me think —No ! for were I to warn Major Wartield ho wouhr absent himself. Should I drop a hint to Marsh she would shrink from the meeting. No; I will lea e it all to Providence; perhaps the sight of her sweet pale face and soft appealing eyes, so full of constancy and truth, may touch that stern old heart. Heaven grant it may r concluded Her- bert Greyson. • • The next day the suit cline on. - At an early hour Dr. Williams appeared, having in eharge Clara Day, who was attended by her friend Mrs. Rocke. They were accommodated with seats immediately in front of 'he judge. Very soon afterwards Major Warfield, Herbert Greyson and Capitola entered, and took their places on the witness's bench, at the- right side of the court-room.

, Herbert watched Old Hurricane, whose eyes were spell-bound to the bench where sat Mrs. Roche and Clara-jßoth - were dressed in deep mourning with n their veils dow and their faces towards the judge. But Herbert dreaded every instant that Multi' Roche should turn her head. and meet that fixed, wistful look. of Old Hurricane. And he wondered what strange instinct it could be that rivetted the old man's regards to that unrecognised woman. At last, to Herbert's great uneasiness, Major Warfield turned and commenced questioning him: "Who is that woman in mourning r " Hem—m -- that one with the flaxen curls under her bonnet is Miss Day." "I don't mean the girl, I mean the woman sit- ting by her ? ' •

"'iliat is—hem—hem !—that is Doctor Williams sitting--" 'Old Hurricane turned abruptly around and favoured his nephew with a severe, scrutinising gaze—demand ing : " 14 erbeo. have you been drinking so early in the morning ? —Demmy, sir ! this is not the season for mint juleps before breakfast 1 Is that great, stout, round bodied, red faced old Doctor Williams a little woman ?—I see him si:ting on the right of Miss Day. I didn't refer ,to him. I referred to that still, quiet little woman sitting on her left, who has never stirred hand or foot since she sat down there, Who is she ?" . ,
"That woman ?—oh l' she 7—yes—ah, let me see —she is a —Miss Day's companion r' faltered Her- bert.

"To the demon with you! who does not see that I —But who is she? What is her name?" abruptly demanded Old Hurricane. "Her name is a—a—Did you ever see her before, air?" "I don't know. That is what I am trying to remember. But, air, will you answer my ques- tion 7" "You seem very much'interested in her." "You seem very mu' h determined not to let me know who she is! Hang it, /air! will you or will , you not, tell. me that woman's name?' Certainly," said Herbert; " her name is—" aboat to say Marah Itocke, but,inoral in- dignation overpowered him,, and he paused. "Well, well, her name is what ? impatiently demanded Old Hurricane. "Mrs. Warfleld !" answered Herbert doggedly. And just at that unfortunate moment Marah turned her pale face and beseechin: eyes around and met the full gaze of herliusband t In an instant her face blanched' to marble and her head sank upen the railing before her bench. Old Hurricane was too dark to grow pale, but his bronzed cheek turned as grey as his hair, which fairly lifted itself on his head. Grasping his walk- ing stick with both his hands he tottered to his feet. and muttering : . "I'll murder you for this, Herbert !" he strode out of the court-room. Marates head rested for alout a minute on the railing before her, and wl,en she lifted it again her face was as calm and patient as before. : ,This little incident had passed without attract- ing attention from anyone except Capitola, who, sitting on the other side of Herbert Greyson, had heard the little passage of words between him and her uncle and had Seen the latter start up and go out, an who now turning to her companion, in- quired : "What is the meaning of alLthis, Herbert?' "It means Satan! AruVriow attend to what is going on. Mr. Slitter has staled the ease, and now Stringfellow, the attorney for the other side, is just telling the judge that he stands there in the place of his client, Lieutenant Glonel Le Noir, who, being ordered to join General Taylor in Mexico, is upon the eve of setting out and cannot be here in person." "And is that true? Won't he be here?" "It seems not. I think he is ashamed to aPPero: after what has happened, and just takes advantage of a fair excuse to absent himself. "..4.114 is he really going te Mexico 2"

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JUNE 13. 1896

"Wet, your great business Was (cone Aere ?mama you And done better for that very reason! No one ever suspected your agency in that matter. The perscn most benefited by the death of Eugene Le Noir was far enough from the scene of his murder I" 'Hush ! perdition seize you! Why do you speak of things so long past I" exclaimed Le Noir, grow- ing while to his very lips. "To jog your worship's memory, and suggest that your honour is the last man who ought to complain of this delay, since it will be very well for you to be in a distant land, serving your coun- try, at the time that your brother's heiress, whose property you illegally hold, is got out of your way." "There is something in that," mused Le Noir. "There is all in that 1" "You have a good brain, Donald !" "What did I tell you ?--I ought to have been in the cabinet, and mean to be too. But Colonel, as I mean to conclude my part of the engagement, I should like for fear of accidents, that you conclude yours—and settle with me before you go." "What do you mean I" "That you should fork over to me the remaining five thousand.' "I'll see you at the demon first," passionately exclaimed Le Noir. "No you won't; for in that case you'd have to make way with the girl yourself; or see Old Hur- ricane make way with all your fortune.' "Wretch, that you are ! "Come, come' Colonel, don't let us quarrel. The Kingdom of Satan divided against itself cannot stand. Do not let us lose time by falling out. / will get rid of the girl! You, before you go, must hand over the tin, lest you should fall in battle and your heirs dispute the debt. Shell out, my Colonel. Shell out, and never fear. Capitola shall be a wife and Black Donald a widower, before many weeks shall pass." "I'll do it. I have no time for disputation, as you know; and you profit by the knowledge. do it, though under protest," muttered Le Noir, grinding his teeth. "That's my brave and generous patron," said Black Donald, as he arose to attend Le Noir from the cavern. "That's my magnificent Colonel of cavalry. The man who runs such risks for you, should be very handsomely remunerated."
CHAPTER XLIV.

div.head: GLORY I
div.p: GLORY I

"What Alexander sighed for What Caesar's soul possessed, What heroes, saints have died for, Glory !" Within three days after tins settlement with Black Donald, Colonel Le Noir left home to join his regiment, ordered to Mexico. He was accompanied by his son, Craven Le Noir as far as Baltimtre, from which port the reinforce- ments were to sail for New OrleanF, en route for the seat of war. _ _

Here, at the last moment, when the ve.sel was about to weigh anchor, Craven le Noir took leave of his father and set out for the Hidden House. Andhere Le Colonel Noir's regiment was joined by the company of new recruits, in which Herbert Greyson held a COMMiS9iOII as lieutenant, and thus the young man's worst forebodings were realised, in having for a travelling companion and superior officer, the man of whom be had been destined to make a mortal enemy, Colonel Le Noir. However, Herbert soon marked out his course of conduct, which was to avoid Le Noir as much as was consis- tent with his own official duty, and when compelled to meet him, to deport himself with the cold ceremony of a subordinate to a superior officer. Le Noir, on his part, treated Herbert with an arrogant scorn amounting to insult, end used every opportunity afforded him by his position to wound and humiliate the young lieutenant. After a quick and prosperous voyage they reached New Orleans, where they expected to be farther reinforced by a company of volunteers who had come down the M'ssissippi riVer from St. Louis. These volunteers were now being daily drilled at their quarters in the city, and were only waiting the arrival of the vessel to be enrolled in the regiment. One morning, a few days after the ship reached harbour, Herbert Greyson went on shore to the military rendtzvous to see the new recruits exer- cised. While he stood within the enclosure watch- ing their evolutions under the orders of an officer, his attention became concentrated upon the form of a yourg man of the rank and file, who was marching in a line with many others having their backs turned towards him. That form and gait seemed familiar—under the circametences in which he saw them again—painfully familiar. And yet he could not identify the man. While he goz,d, the recruits, at the word of command, suddenly wheeled and faced about. And Herbert could scarcely repress an exclamation of astonishment and regret. That young man in the dress of a private soldier was Clara Day's betrothed, the widow's only son, Traverse lbcke I While Herbert continecd to gaze In surprise and gi ler, the young iecruit raised his eycs, recoan z.,d his friend, fleshed up to his very temples and cast his eyes thown again. The rapid evolutions soon wheeled them around, and the next order sent th,-m into their quarters. _ .

Hubei t's time was also up, and he returned to his duty. The next day llerbort went to the quarters of the tvw recruits, and sought oat his young friend, whom he found loitering about the grcunds. Again Travcr a blushed deeply as the young lieutenant appro,tched. But Herbert Gre7eon, letting none of his regret appear. since now it would be worse than ust-les,, in only serving to cive pain to the young private, went up to him cordially and shook his bands, saying : tc, serve your country, eh, Traverse ? Well. I am heartily glad to see you, at any rate." " Bat heartily sorry to see me here, enlisted as a' private in a company of raw recruits, looking not unlike Ird.lst:iff's ragged recriment 1" " Nay. I did not say that, Traverse. Mary a private in tine ranks has risen to be a general officer," replied Herbert, encouragingly. Traverse laughed good humoredly, saying: "Is does not look much like that in my case. This dress," he said, looking down at his coarse, ill- fitting uniform, cow-hide shoes, etc.—" this dress, this drilling. these clew.) quarters, coarse food, and mixed company, is enough to take the military ardour out of anyone." "Traverse, you talk like a dandy, which is not at all your character. Effeminacy is not your vice." "Nor any other species of weakness, do you mean? Ah, Herbert! your aspiring, hopeful, con- fident old friend is considerably taken down in his ideas of himself, his success, and life in general. I went to the West with high hopes. Six months of struggling aga'nst indifference, neglect and accu- mulating debts, lowered them down. I carried out letters and made friends, but their friendship began and ended in wishing me well. While trying to get into profitable practice I got into debt. Meanwhile I could not hear from my betrothed in all those months. An occasional letter from her might Dave prevented this step. But troubles gathered around me, debts increased, and----" "Creditors were cruel. It is the old story, poor

boy ! " "No; my only creditors were my landlady and my laundress, two poor widows who never wiilingly distressed me, but who occasionally asked for 'that little amount' so piteou,ly that my heart bled to lack it to give them. And as vi.ctuals and clean shirts were absolate necessaries of life, every week my debts increased. I could have faced a prosper- ous male creditor, and might, perhaps, have been provoked to bully such an one, had he been inclined to be cruel; but I could not face poor women, who after all. I believe, are generally the best friends a struggling young man can have; and so, not to bore a emait young lieutenant with a poor private's antecedents—" "Oh, Traverse—" —" I will even make an end of my story. 'At last there came a weary day when hope and faith beneath the weight gave way.' And hearing that a company of volunteers was being raised to go to Mexico. I enlisted, sold my citizen's wardrobe and my little medical library, paid my debts, made my two friends, the poor widows, some acceptable presents, sent the small remnant of the money to my mother telling her that I was going farther south to try my fortune, and—here I am I "You did not tell her that you had enlisted?" "No." "Oh, Traverse! how long ago was it that you left St. Louis?" "Just two weeks." "Abi if you had only had patience for a few days longer I " burst unaware from Herbert's bosom. In an instant he was sorry for having spoken thus, for Traverse, with all hi a soul in his eyes, asked eagerly: "Why—why Herbert? What do you mean ? " "Why. you should know that I did net come direct from West Point, but from the neighbour- hood of Staunton and Hurricane Hall." "Did you? oh, did you Then you may be able to give me news of Clara and my dear mother 11' exclaimed Traverse eagerly. "Yes, I am--pleasant news," said Herbert, hesi- tating in a manner in which no one ever hesitated befog iq,comtwicAtirix Kciod_ tiding _

"-manic season I on, tnanz maven TV ria-c Herbert? How is my dear mother getting on? Where is my best Clara 7 " "They are both living together at Willow Heights, according to the wishes of the late Doctor Day. A second appeal to the Orphans' Court, made in be- half of Clara by her next friend, Doctor Williams, about a month ago, proved more successful. And If you had waited a few days longer before enlisting and leaving St. Louis, you would have received a letter from Clara to the same effect, and oRe from Doctor Willilms, apprising you that your mother had received her legacy, and that the thousand dollars left you by Doctor Day had been paid into the Agricultural Bank, subject to your orders." "Oh, Heaven I had I but waited three days longer 1" exclaimed Traverse, in such acute distress that Herbert hastened to console him by saying:

"Do not repine, Traverse. These things io by fate. It was your destiny—let us hope it will prove a glorious one." "It was my IMPATIENCE!" exclaimed Traverse. "It was my IMPATIENCE Doctor Day always faithfully warned me against it—always told me that m3st of the errors, sins and miseries of this world arose from simple impatience, which is want of faith. And now I know it I and now I know it! What had /, who had an honourable profession, to do with becoming a private.soldier 2"

"Well, well, it-is lconourable at least to serve your country," said Herbert, soothingly. "If a foreign foe invaded her shores, yes; but what had I to do with invading another's country 7 enlisting for a war of the rights and wrongs of which I know no more than anybody else does! Growing impatient because fortune did not at once empty her cornucopia upon my head 1 Oh, fool 1"

'You blame yourself too severely, Traver.se. Your act was natural enough and justifiable enough, much as it is to be regretted," said Herbert cheer- fully. " Come, come, sit on this blank bench beside me —if you are not ashamed to te seen with a private who is also a donkey—and tell me all about it. Show me the full measure of the happiness I have so recklessly squandered away," exclaimed Traverse, des pel a tely. "I will sit beside you and tell you everything you wish to know—on condition that you stop berating yourself in a manner that fills me with indignation," replied Herbert, as they went to a distant part of the dusty enclosure and took their seats upon a rude bench.

"Oh, Herbert, bear with me; I could dash my wild, impatient bead against a stone wall I" "That would not be likely to clear or stengthen your brains," said Herbert, who thereupon com- menced and told Traverse the whole history of the persecution of Clara Day at the Hidden House; the interception of her letters • the attempt made to force her into a marriage with Craven La Noir ; her deliverance from her enemies by the address and courage of Capitola ; her flight to Staunton and refuge with Mrs. Rocke ; her appeal to the court; and finally her success and her settlement under the charge of her matronly friend at Willow Heights. Traverse had not listened patiently to this account. He heard it with many bursts of irre- pressible indignation and many involuntary starts of wild passion. Towards the last he sprang up and down, chafing like an angry lion in his cage. "And this man," he exclaimed, as Hebert con- cluded,—" This demon—this beast—is now com- manding officer! the colonel of our regiment " "Yes," replied Hebert, "but as such you must not call him names; military rules are despotic: and this man who knows your person and knows you to be the betrothed of Clara Day, whose hand and fortune he covets for his son will leave no power with which his command invests him, untried, to ruin and destroy you Traverse, I say these these things to you, that being forewarned ' you may be forearmed.' I trust that you will remember your mother and your betrothed, and for their dear sakes practice every sort of self-control, patience and for- bearance under the provocations you may receive Vora our colonel. And in advising you to do this, I only counsel that which I shall myself practice. too, am under the ban of Le Noir for the part I played in the church in succouring Capitola. as well as for happening to be the nephew of my uncle,' Major Warfield, who is his mortal enemy." "1 ?—will I not be patient, after the lesson I have just learned upon the evils of its opposite? Be easy on my account, dear old friend. I will be as patient as ob, meek as Moses, and long suffering as—my own sweet mother!" said Traverse, earnestly. The drum was now heard beating to quarters, and Traverse, wringing his friend's hid, left hi m.

Hobert returned to his ship full of one scheme, of which he had not spoken to Traverse Ist it it should prove unsuccessfal. This scheme was to procure his free discharge before they should set sail for the Itio Grande. He had many influential friervlt; among the officers of his regiment, and he was resolved to tell them as much as was delicxtc, proper and useful for them to know of the :;.ourg, recruit's private history in ordcr to get their co- operation. Herbert spent every hour of this day and the next, when off duty, in this service of his frind. He found his brother-olVers eaolly interested, sym- pathetic and propitious. They united their !efforts with his own to procure the discharge of the young recruit ; but in vain! the power of Colonel Le Noir was opposed to their influence, and the application was peremptorily refused. - Herbert Greyson did not sit down quietly under this disappointment, but wrote an application, en- bodying all the facts of the case to the Secretary of War, got it signed by all the officers of the regiment and dispatched it by the first mail. Simultaneously he took another important step for the interest of his friend. Without hinting any particular motive he had begged Traverse to let him have his photograph taken, and the latter, with a length at the lover-like proposal, had consented. When the likeness was finished, Hebert sent it by express to Major Warfield, accompanied by a letter describing the excellent character and unfortunate condition of Traverse, praying the Major's interest in his behelf, and concluded by saying: "You cannot look upon the accompanying photo- graph of my friend and any longer disclaim your own express image in your son." - How this affected the action of Old Hurricane will be seen hereafter. Traverse, knowing nothing of the efforts that had been, and were still being made for his discharge, suffered neither disappointment for failure of the first, nor anxiety for_the issue of the last. - He wrote to his mother and Clara, con- gratulating them on their good fortune; tell- ing them that he, in common with many young men of St. Louis, had volunteered for the Mexican War ; that he was then at New Orleans, en route for the Rio Grande, and that they would be pleased to know that their mutual friend Herbert Greyson, was an officer in the same regiment of which he himself was at present a,private, but with strong hopes of soon winning his- epaulettes. He endorsed an order for his mother to draw the thousand dollars left him by Doctor Day; and be advised her to redeposit the sum in her own name, for her own use in case of need. Praying God's blessing upon them all, and begging their prayers for himself, Traverse concluded his letter, which he mailed the same evening. And the next morning the company was ordered on board, and the whole expedition set sail for the Rio Grande.

Now we mit2ht just as easily as not accompany the troops to Mexico and relate the feats of arms there performed, with the minuteness and fidelity of an eye-witness, since we have sat at dinner tables where the heroes of that war have been honoured guests, and where we have heard them fight their battles over till "thrice the foe was slain, and thrice the field was won."

We might follow the rising star or our young lieutenant, as by his own merits and other's mishaps he ascended from rank to rank, through all the grades of military yromotion, but we need not, because the feats of Lieutenant—Captain—Major and Colonel Grevson are they not written in the chronicles of the Mexican war?

We prefer to look alter our little domestic heroine, our brave little Cap, who, when women have their rights, shall be a lieutenant-colonel herself. Shall she not gentlemen? In one fortnight from this time, while Mrs. Rocke and Clara were still living comfortably at Willow Heights, and waiting anxiously to hear from Traverse, whom they still supposed to be practising his profession at' St. Louis, they received his last letter written on the eve of his departure for the seat of war. At first the news overwhelmed them with grief, but then' they sought relief in faith, answered hi.; letter cheerfully, and commended him to the Efinite mercy of god. (To be eontin.tied. )

The leading rne —7-the Church party in Parliament are in nlvebersl o w spirits over the fate of the Benefices Bill.rYnole unblushing il a_vocacy, or something like it, of the traffic in souls on the part of one or two and t members on the Governmehnte side is in particular very much deplored. Church party recognise that unless the Govern- 13.ent come to their aid there is no hope for the bill. It seems impossible that the Committee stage Should be concluded on Thursday, and this modest measure in the direction of Church reform will tonsequently again be shelved, mainly through the Opposition of those who regard the preservation of vested interests as a paramount consideration. Gireat pressure will be brought to bear upon Mr. Balfour to grant time for the consideration of the bill, but with the business of the Rouge already so Much in arrear, it is not thought likely that the application will be successful.

The Queen was awarded a Banksian medal at the Royal Horticultural Society's Show on Tuesday for 4 splendid exhibit of strawberries, including 'some of the largest kinds grown. The latest Derby win- ner was immortalised in the name of a new "regal Pelargonium," deep crimson in colour and labelled 'Persimmon?' Like its namesake, the new bloom Carried a blue ribbon, an honeur shared by the grower of a beautiful single peony with remark- ably full anthers. Another feature of the show was the presence of the old-lashioned blue larkspur in unusual abundance, a fact which lovers of by-gone 'gardens may take to portend a restoration of one of t.he most brilliant denizens of country pleasaunces 111 past generations. A collection of single briar roses which attracted a good deal of notice included a flue copper-coloured variety which was wonder- ully . effective.

The Committee on the Unemoloyed have con- sidered a number of points submitted to them by the chairman, Mr. T. W. Russell, as the basis of a report. These included recommendations in regard to farm colonies and other plans for permanently Rrappling with the existing distress in large towns. The suggestions of the chairman were generally adopted, and there is every prospect of a unani- raoUB report.

the scandal of the exclusion of the Roman 'Catholic. of Belfast from all representation on the t corporation of that. city—is, at last, likely to be abated. The Corporatkn of Belfast are promoting A Bill for the extension of their borough boundaries. la the extended municipality the old order of 19things was to be continued ; but the Parliamentary onitnittee to whom the Bill was referred were so 111.2 Pressed by the case presented to them on behalf tit the Catholics that they intimated that unless /lame representation for the prescribed creed on the corporation was provided by the Bill they could not report it to the House. There was a strong feeling accongst the extreme Orange section of Belfast that t_he Bill should be dropped rather than Roman uatholics should obtain a voice in the management of the affairs of the city. But happily, more liberal s a'acl tolerant counsels have prevailed, and a scheme Which wa drawn up by a sub-committee of the e°rPoration and the representatives of the Catholics and approved by the town council, will be embodied the ill. by which the Catholics will be able to "withuN "'Jo representatives of two out of the fifteen This means that the Catholics will have cePresentatives in the town council. But then eile(Y, are one-fourth ot the population,and the Coun- oaf-"siBts of sixty members, so that, after all, it is Y small mercies for which they have to be oankful.

A faymii.i trimming for summer hats is a wreath of cherry fotiage, and a large bunch of red cherries at the side, With, Perhaps, a knot of ribbon inter- mixed. Large margusrites, in white, black, and yellow, on a white hat veiled with leaf-green tulle, are also suitable for the present season. A com- bination of blue .and green, ,in shot straws and mixed tulle trimmings, is still in favour, and there is no doubt that this combination is a very-becom- .. kffir

nig one, if the real peacock shades are chosen. A charming hat has a crown, shaped somewhat after thd Italian headgear style, it standing out• Square in front and rising at the back, where it is filled in with flowers. style of. trimming that I -Sug- gest is equally.snitc,i to any' of the round or oblong shape toque, which cannoty.be had in a variety of coarse straws.

Some extremely pretty frocks for children and young girls are being made in spotted and printed nuislins and silk zephyrs, abd, after all, there is nothirig nicer :for young people, than washing materials' for, with a good supply of warm Under- clothing for cold days they can be worn right through the summer, and can take a fresh lease of life at the cleaner's when they have lost their first freshness.

For morning wear, coats and skirts in pale fawn cloths with over-cuffs and revers of blue face cloth, or in serge or covert coating are just as popu- lor with the children as they are with their elders, and very pretty little cambric blouses, with large collars, edged with lace or goffered frills, can now be brought ready-made. Cream serge skirts or navy blue skirts either in alpaca or serge, are also made specially for wearing with these blouses when an entire costume of a coat and skirt is not desired. Fancy washing flannel blouses, in Pompadour pat- tern, are nice for cycling and tennis, and these are made in very comfortable shapes, suitable for tak- ing exercise in. _ _ _

The latest fashion, however, is to wear corsets of fine batiste, embroidered with conventional designs in silk, such as a black ground, with turquoise-blue fleur de lye on it, and ribbon trim- mings to match. These fragile-looking corsets are, strange to say, more durable than silk or satin, and are therefore, more often chosen for everyday wear. Fancy embroidered coutil is also very use- ful, and this, of course, is the most durable of all. most people with perfectly normal figures wear ready-made corsets nowadays, for these have been brought to such perfection that they are (pito satisfactory for anyone of normal proportions. There are, however, many people who differ slightly in their proportions, and in such cases it is absolutely necessary to have corsets made to measure.

There is probably on dress materia at is so universally popular as serge, and this is not to be wondered at, seeing that it makes such stylish and useful gowns for all occasions w here good wearing materials are required, and now that women take so much interest in outdoor sports and pastimes, it is more popular than ever. Besides the ordinary blue, white, and red serges, some attractive mater- ials in grey and natural wool shades will be found among the patterns, and these are highly rnorn- mended, because they wear splendidly, and do not show the dust so much as dark materials. A coat and skirt worn by a very pretty dark woman, who evidently knows how to dress, is of dark green free cloth with a white satin lining and revers of putty-coloured cloth, have three cress- cut bands of white satin laid on them; the full front is of mauve crêpe de chine set into innumer- able tucks running across the figure, and her hat is a green straw swathed with green and mauve tulle, and further adorned with green wings. Your loving JENNIE.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, :z;ATTTRDAY, JUNE 13, 1896.
WHAT WOULD THE CODFISH SAY?

The codfish in the scas realise how great -a blessing they are to mankind, they would not mind so much be- ing caught, and dried and salted. At least, this is one way of looking at it. The cil alone which is made from their livers has probably saved more lives than any- body will ever realise. Most of its wonderful benefits are " born to blush unseen." Fortunately, some of them are not, and may thereby accomplish much good. Here is a case we are enabled to publish _ _

" In May, 1890,1 had a very severe attack of influenza which left both lungs weak. Each winter since I have had bad attacks of bronehitis or inflammation, my lungs getting worse and worse, until I found myself in January, 1895, quite unfit for my occupation, and had to give up my situation. The doctor pronounced it con- sumption, and ordered me to Clifton, where I was dur- ing February and March, without any benefit. About this time a friend sent me a bAtle of Scott's Emulsion, asking me to try it. I did so, and thought I felt slightly better. The phlegm became less and the night sweats less frequent. In April I went into Devonshire, my I friends were thinking I had come to die, as I was so weak. Goo I nursing, and the regular use ef Scott's Emulsion, soon gave me strength,and I rapidly gained weight—over nine pounds in two months I was ordered here for the wiuter,and I am glad to say that so far I have been entirely free from all colds, and am feel- ing stronger than I have for more than a year p ist. I hope with the regular use of Scott's Emulsion .o be able to resume work in a month or two. For seven months have taken no other meclicine,although I am under the care of a doctor here. I told him. what I was taking,and he said :" C intinue taking it,as it agrees with vou. I is a capital preparation,and to you is both medicine and food." There are many cases like mine. They cinnot take the raw cod-liver oil,but if they tried Scott's Emul- sion, would find they could easily digest it, and if they began taking it in time, would gain strength, instead of gradually sinking away.—Yours very sincerely (signed) EDMUND D. JORY, 3 Belvedere, Lincoln &venue, Bournemouth, January 28h, 1896." It is interesting to know that Scott's Emulsion is a perfectly palatable preparation. It presents cod liver oil in an easy form for digestion and assimilation, and combines with it the hypophosphites of lime and soda in such a peculiar way that the potency of each is increased. In no other preparation can be foucd th;s ideal combin- ation, and in no other preparation is there such perfect manipulation of the oil. This is why Scott's Emulsion is effective in cases where other forms of cod-liver oil have proved useless. A trial of Scott's Emulsion will convince you of its superlative merit. You can always distinguish the genuine by the unique trade-mark of a man carrying a big fish on his back, which is on the wrapper of every genuine bottle. (16)
THE TRIPLE EXECUNON.
FOWLER, MILSOM, AND SEAMAN HANGED AT NEWGATE. THEIR LAST MOMENTS.

Three of the four murderers sentenced to death at the last sittings of the Central Criminal Court by Mr. Justlce flawkins,were executed on Tuesday morning at Newgate Prison. Henry Fowler, thirty-one, and Albert Milsom, thirty-three,were executed for the murder of Mr. Henry Smith at Nluswell Lodge in February last ; and William Seaman,forty-six, a diver, for the murder of John Good- man Levy and Mrs. Gale in Wititechapel. There were present at the execution Colonel Miltnan, the Governor of Newgate ; Mr. Ruston, Uncler-Sneriff of Middlesex ; Mr. Metcalfe,Under-Sheriff of London; Major Campbell, Deputy-Governor of Holloway ; Dr. Pitcairn and Dr. Scott,the medical officers of the gaol ; and the Revs. G. P. Merrick and A. K. Ramsay, chaplains. There was also a strong extra force of warders on duty in anticipa- tion of further violent " scenes." Billington was the executioner, and he was assisted by Wilkinson. of Bolton. The sheriffs de- cided to exclude the Press, and the authorities at Newgate have been very reticent as to what took place in the condemned cells since the trial. It is stated, however, that when Colonel Milman and the under- sheriffs went to Fowler's cell with the executioners on Tuesday morning, the culprit appeared quite prepared for their coining, and having shaken hands with Mr.' Billington. he submitted quietly to the pinioning. Sea- man and Milsom were next visited,and a procession was then formed,Fowler leading, and Milsom corning last, the three doomed men, who marched in stolid silence, being surrounded by warders. When the chalk line marked on the drop in the corner of the shed to indicate a plump line with the rope above was pointed out to Fowler as his position to stand he quickly advanced, bringing his feet down heavily in the place indicated. While Billington was strapping his legs together the cul- prit threw his head back and gazed about him with evi- dent interest. Before Milsom had entered the shed the white cap had been drawn over Fowler's head and his bared neck, and the mese of the rope adju ted. Mean- while Wilkinson had prepared Sstamau in a like manner, and Milsom was prepared fs r a drop in the space of a few seconds. Billington tilting a cursory survey of all the arrangements, stepped aside, touched the lever, and. the floor gave way, the chaplain meanwhile reciting the Burial Service. Tne following is the official statement made by the two under-sheriffs as to what toiak place: —" There was no scene on the scaffold oetween the prisoners Fowler and Milsom. Fowler declined to make ' any statement whatever. Milsom said. lam perfectly innocent. lam not guilty of the crime.' Seaman, who volunteered no statement, was asked if he wished to say anything. He replied, No, sir ; I have nothing what- ever to say.'" There was a great crowd outside the prison as early as seven o'clock on Tuesday incirning„ and it grew to such large proportions before nine o'clock,that the police had some difficulty in regulating the traffic. The p bhic- houses in the vicinity were crowded, and appeared to be doing a roaring trade, In fact very few of those present seemed to pay much attention to the solemnity of the scene which was being enacted inside the gaol. There was a good deal of chaff and rough horseplay, and the whole scene led to the reflection as to whether Newgate was the best or most seemly place to carry out the extreme lanalty of the law. The aboli- tion of public executions has not, even after the lapse of more than a quarter of a century. done away with the morbid interest which people take in great criminals. At a quarter to nine the bell of St. Sepulchre's began to tell,and this added to the excitement of the crowd. Then the chapel bell within the gaol began to toll, and at five minutes to nine there were speculations as to whether another "scrap" was going on at the gallows between Fowler and Milso:n. The former seemed to be almost regarded as a hero.but the remarks about the latter were emphatically not fit for publication. Slowly the minutes wore away, and the crowd grew silent when St.Sepul- chre's clock began to strike the hour. Almost before the echoes of the last stroke had died away, a square of black bunting was seen slowly ascending the pole over the prison. This was an intimation that t%e law had been vindicated,and a hoarse roar of cheering from the crowd seemed to drown the noise of the traffic for a moment. Then the people rushed away about their business.

EXECUTION OF .MRS. DYER. Mrs. Dyer, condemned to death tor killing two infants named MarmOn and himmons at Reading. was hanged at Newgate on Wednesday. The murders for which she suffered were but two incidents ij a long carer of crime. The evidence the police were able to coll.ct led to the belief that for years the wretched woman had taken in children to nurse, that in each case she had taken in a premium, and that in a great number of cases she had ended the chi,d's life by tying a piece of

„ tape so tightly round it ne± as to cause strangulation. She caused her own arrest and subsequent conviction by one of those oversights so common in the annals ot crime. Her habit was to wrap UP the bodies of her victims in parcels, fasten a stone to the bundle, and then drop it into a river. A child's body enclosed in a brown paper was found, with a tape still around its neck, and on the brown paper were the name and ad- dress of the murderess.

div.head: "WOMEN'S CHAT:"
div.p: "WOMEN'S CHAT:"

The .The wine Room e hicle was held on Wednesday, th'lO:r.., by rte. Priecees of Wale, on behalf cf Her Mi .•e4 e eat e; peonlarly known as a•" Consola- tioe hie Room. Between three andJour hundred women were disappointed at the last Drawing ItOom,ow- ing te the regulation number of debutantes being limited to 200, and they would have had to wait until next year had it not been for the Queen's consideration in decie- ing upon an extra function this season. About fifteen hundred invitations will be issued by the Lord Chamberlain for each of ' those depressing Royal ceremonies, viz.. the State concerts; which are to be given it Buckingham Palace ,on the 22nd and 29th of i this month. The Court Balls, none of which,by the way, will take place this year, owing to the death of Prince Henry' of Battenberg, are not particularly enlivening, but they are festive ,occasions compared with a State ,concert. At the former function there is "a certain amount of subdued gaiety, but at the musical. 'gather- ing a chilly sense.of doing penance pervades the whole assemblage. The programme presented is of course al- ways:excellent and the artistes of the first rank, but the applause is strictly decorqul; talking and tabooed, and when the entertainment is at an end, the guests file out with as much solemnity as though they were in church. The young Duchess of Marlborough, by her corres- pondence which includes scores upon scores of letters osking, her to open or otherwise patronise bazaars, can only suppose this particular ferm of mingled charity and amusement to be reckoned Upon if you come to live in all Eastern—a comparatively Eastern land. Her Grace is. of course, for the moinent, the greatest " draw " that can be found, and thus the children of light are wise enough to see. The very latest thing in wedding gowns is silk muslin embroidered in pearls and trimmed with sprays of orange blossom. This womover white silk, is a thou- sand times more becoming to the average bride than the usual white satin. Shower bouquets for brides are still the only wear.though I have seen a trellis. This suggests ' more than the trails of greenery and blossom.for it has a I ladder like effect and is shorter than the ordinary trail. Speaking of weddings reminds me of the fact that honeymoons used to hit a month or longer, now they grow shorter and shorter, and a fornight is, at the pre- sent time considered quite a long one. I Leghorn hats which are high is favour just now, are almost pastoral with their wreath of roses and " dipp- ing "flexible brim,—the narrow black velvet strings giving a pretty finish to the ensemble. There is a touch of the Dresden China Shepherdess about these particu- lar hats that make them deliciously becoming to youth- ful faces, especially when worn slightly on one side raised by a half wreath of flowers resting on the hair. The: eis no doubt that if women understood better the value of a background, to throw beauty into relief, they would exercise more time and thought in the selec- tion of wall-paper. In some rooms a woman looks her best, in others her worst. All papers should be well considered in artificial, as well as day light, a large piece being pinned to the wall of the rooom in which it is to be hung. There are some papers that are quite impossible to live with and these are often the most charming to lgok upon in the pattern book. Diatemper has of late been largely adopted in. lieu of wall-papers, and the ceiling made to repeat the colour of the walls, but unless a plentiful array of pictures is available the room wears an aspect of utter desolation. Among many other good things, we owe paper wall coverings to Queen Mary 11. and her Dutch husband, William of Orange. Paper hanging of a kind had cer- tainly been used before, but the design usually consisted of maps of different parts of the 'world surrounded by fantastic borders. The wall papers which were first used in this reign for decorating some of the apartments in Kensington Palace resembled the flock designs so popular a few years since. Their cleanliness and cheap- ness compared with the tapestry,satin, or damask hang. logs previously employed, soon brought them into general use, and now they have spread over the lengt h and breadth of the land and their manufacture repre- sents an inn ortant branch of industry, giving employ- ment to many thousands of hands. Those sufferers from street noises,who are not already aware of the fact, will be interested to know that in order to be rid of the sounding brass of the German band or the tinkling cymbal and shrill voiced strains of the Salvationist, they must plead either that they are toe ill to enjoy (?) the music, or that it interferes with their ordinary occupation or pursuit. The present act gives us a further vogue right to our peace at home by the clause" for other reasons or for a sufficient cause, but their good reason may not appear a sufficient cause to the organ grinder or bandsmen from the " Happy Fatherland." At present one may have one's evening after dinner rendered hideous by street noises, unless, indeed one happens to be ill in bed, or at work in one's study. It seems the Americans, weary of orchids and costly flowers of all kinds,have pronounced the potato blossom first in Flora's kingdom for the time. Boston leads the way and is decorating its rooms and its dinner tables with the lowly little bloom. This is indeed a reaction. The land of millionaires ,is tired of beauty which can merely be bought with money ! However, the worship of the potato blossom, is, after all, more elevating than the cult of the green carnation. Apropoe it is said that the very first crop of potatoes raised in England was at Formby, on the Lancashire coast, by a native of that village. This particular vegetable was imported by Sir Walter Raleigh in the reign of Queen Elizabeth. The extraordinary decrease in 'English feminine crim- inals is indeed a fact to rejoice over. Eighteen years ago the female erisen at Woking, holding eight !hundred prisoners was quite full, now the only prison for women, which has been built at Aylesbury,em hold three hundred women, at the present moment contains but two hun- dred. In France. of 4,269 accused persons in 1893.3,873 were men, and 596 women, a proportion of six to one. In other words, woman was responsible for 14 per cent. of the crimes committed, a diminution since the period comprised between the years 1871-76, when the percent- age was 17. Here are a few rules we should all do well to follow. with regard to sea-bathing. Avoid bathing when exhausted by fatigue, avoid bathing within two hours after a meal. Avoid bathing when the body is cooling after perspiration hut bathe when the body is warm provided .no time is lost in getting into the water. Avoid remainine too long in the water, leave it immediately there is the slightest feeling of chilliness. Avoid bathing altogether in the open air, if after having been a short time in the water there is a sense of chilliness, with numbness of the bands and feet. The vigorous and strong may bathe early in the morning before breakfast, but the young and those whoare weak should bathe two or three hours after. Gooseberry Souffiee is delicious,easily made,and inex- pensive. Cook one pint of gooseberries with water to cover and sugar to taste. Rub them through a hair sieve, and leave until cold. When cold add two ounces of fine bread crumbs end the yolks of three eges,beatine them one by one. Whip the whites to a stiff froth,add them lightly to the gooseberries, and turn all into a _ buttered tin or pie dish. en for aliout _ Bake in a hot oven

half an hour, and serve immediately. Many of my correspondents seem troubled concerning their hair falling out ppit now. One of the best remedies I know is eval quant;tiPs of almond oil and eau de Cologne,', and a few drops of cantharides well shaken up together. If the hal,. is dry increase the oil,if moist in- crease the eau de Cologne.
