div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
MONDAY,

Answering Colonel R-u-s-sell in the House of Commons yesteriay, Mr. BRODRICK expressed his regret that the delay in passing the Military Manceuvres Bill would necessitate the abandonment for the prevent year of mar ceuvres on an extended scale which the military authorities had impressed upon the Government as es- sential for the proper training of the army. Even if the bill fell through to the extent that the money voted by Parliament could not be made available for manceu- vres in the present year, he should certainly press it later in the session, having regard to the fact that this country was alone among the nations of Europe in hav- ing no facilities for the training of its troops. Questioned by Sir R. Reid as to the steps the Govern- ment had taken to prevent a repetition in Crete of the massacres recently perpetrated in Armenia, Mr. CURZON said that so long ago as December last the English Am- bassador at Constantinople was instructed to call the attention of ths Turkish Government to the state of affairs in Crete, and to impress upon them the danger of serious trcuble unless some remedial measures were soon adopted. Those friendly representations had been more than once renewed. Recently the English Consul in Crete had been instructed, in conjunction with his colleagues, to enter into negotiations with the Turkish authorities and with the local leaders in order to pre- vent the occurrence of excesses and to facilitate a peace- ful settlement of the question. Mr. CURSON informed zir W. 11. Houldsnrorth that the Foreign Office had received no intimation that twenty- three of the leading Indian merchants at Kilwa, in Ger- man East Africa, had been executed for alleged com- plicity in a rebellious rising in that district. In reply to Mr. Fenwick, Sir M. WHITE RILEY said he was encouraged by the feeling in all quarters of the House on the subject of the Coal Mines Bill to hope that the HOOPS would agree to the second reading of the bill, if confined exclusively to the parts which dealt with the safety of the mines, without debate, with a view of its being referred to the Grand Committee en Trade. Mr. Hedderwick, the new member for the Wick Burghs, took his seat. TUESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday Captain DoNELax,on behalf of Mr. T. P. O'Connor,asked whether the Government had any information as to the truth of the statements that a brisk trade was being carried on by the Turkish soldiers in Crete in the spoils plundered from Cretan villages, that a portion of the troops des- patched to Crete were the same who committed the horrorsin Armenia, and that some of these soldiers were reported to be selling watches, earrings, and revolvers taken from the Armenians. Mr. Comm replied that the Government had no official confirmation of the news- paper reports mentioned in the question. Ihe British Consul, however, having heard that some of the troops recently at Zeitun had been sent to Crete, made special representation to the Vail en the subject. Mr. P. STANHOPE asked the Secretary for the Colonies whether his attention bad been drawn to the account given from Bulawayo of the battle of the 6th inst., in which it was said that the " rebels " were shot down under the horses' hoofs, no quarter being given or asked for, and whether Sir F. Carrington was now solely in charge of tbe military operations, or whether the Char- tered Company was responsible for these alleged severi- ties. Mr. CflamnenTAlN said he had seen the report re- ferred to. Mr. F. Carrington had sole charge of all the military operations, and he was no doubt responsible, as commanding officer,to do his utmost to ensure that the operations were conducted according to the usages of war,but he (Mr. Chamberlain) was afraid that it was impossible to give quarter to an armed enemy w.‘o was not disabled and who did not ask for quarter. Answering Sir C. Dilke, Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH said it would not be necessary, pending appeal, to find for the Egyptian operations in the Soudan and for the Indian expedition to Suakim moneys other than those held by the Mixed Tribunal to have been illegally ad- vanced from the Reserve Fund. The extraordinary ex- penses of the Indian garrison at Suakim would be de- frayed out of the Treasury chest, but in what way the Treasury chest would be repaid was a subject for fur- ther consideration. He adhered to the statement in his Budget speech, when, of course, he did not antici- pate the decision of the Tribunal. That decision was subject to an appeal,and he had every hope it would be reversed.

The House went into Committee of Supply on the Irish Estimates. On the vote for the Royal Irish Con- stabulary Mr. SWIFT MACNEILL complained of the great increase in the cost of the force of recent years. He also urged that the men should be numbered,so as to enable people to ideaufp them. Mr. W. REDMOND moved the reduction of the vote by £500,000. Mr. G. BALFOUR re- plying on the debate, said it would be Ws endoavour to diminish the number of extra police in any district. The large expenditure on the police force was largely due to the pension fund, which was now added to the other expenditure. Wages had also risen in all departments. It was unfortunate that the spasmodic rise and fall of crime in Ireland made it necessary to keep a police force , which appeared to be larger than the necessities of the I country demanded. As to the proposal that some dis- tinguishing mark should be placed on the uniform of the constabulary, he could not, "as at present advised," consent to such a mark being used. After an attempted "count out" the amendment was rejected by 156 votes to 70, and the vote WAR agreed to. WEDNESDAY.

On Wednesday in thellouse of -Commons the Benefices Bill as amended by the Standard Committee was again considered. The discussion of Lord Cranberne's amend- ment to provide that the transfer of a right of patronage made within nine months after the institution of an in- cumbent to a benefice to which the right of patronage related should be void was resumed, and eventually the amendment was carried by 112 votes to 55. Mr. S. Evens proposed that the prohibition against a transferer exercising his right within nino months should not ap: ply to a person at the point of death who wished to de- vise the right. This was rejected by 136 votes to 61. The omission of sub-section 3 was moved by Mr. H. Fosma, who subsequently withdrew the motion. Mr. CARVELL WILLIAMS moved an amendment for the pur- pose of prohibiting any payment whatever in connection with the transfer of patronage rights, but it was re- jected by 177 votes to 115. Two or three other amend- ments were also rejected. hut at half-past five, when business must cease, the first clause of the Bill was still under consideration, and there remained twenty other dances to discuss.

div.p: MR. ,T USTI() PIS VIRLING AND DR. WILLIAMS' PINK PILLS. IMPORTANT DECISION.

In the High Court of Chancery, recently, Mr. Justice Stirling granted an Injunction (with costs) against a London chemist, which is of much public importance. The terms of the order are" that the defendant,George Goss, his servants awl agents, be perpetually restrained from supplying to persons who ask for or order Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, under that or any abbreviated title such as Pink Pills for Pale People,' ' Dr. Williams' Pink Pills,' or Dr. Williams' Pills,' any pillsnot being the Plaintiff's Pills, and also from passing off such pills lay the use of the term Pink Pills for Bloodless People,' or in any other way." The defendant is also required to give up to the plaintiff all labelsokc. containing the term "Pink Pills for Bloodless People," and account to the plaintiff for all profits made by the illegal use of that title. The numerous cures effected in this country by Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale Pec pie have led to fraudu- lent substitutions being attempted. Anyone who knows of such substitution, or attempted substitution, is asked to communicate (in strict confidence) with Mr. C. Urquhart Fisher, 45, Holborn-Viaduct, London, E.C., solicitor to the manufacturers of the genuine Pills, who will take legal proceedings for the enforcement of the Company's rights.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WA.RRINGTON.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WA.RRINGTON.
WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY.

The weekly meeting of this society held in Wycliffe Church on Sunday afternoon was presided over by Mr. Thomas Wallington, the hon. secretary. In the five minutes alloted to him for an address, he spoke of the prevalence of impure speech in the town. It was to be heard in the streets, in the workshops, and offices, and he urged the members of the P.S.A. to set a good ex- ample to their fellows in this respect by keeping their lips pure from the bad language which they so often heard.—The address for the afternoon was delivered by Mr. William Beswick, of Warrington, who, in a most in- teresting manner, drew some useful lessons from the life of Joseph in Egypt. The soloist was Mr. George Gough who sang the hymn" Behold me standing at the door," and also "Behold I stand at the door." Mr. W. H. Pay- ton presided at the organ. Mr. Thomas Hawthorn and Mr. Seeley also assisted in the service.

PUBLIC MEETING AT BuLD- STRE CHURCH.

Councillor J. SHILW GREEN proposed a vote of thanks 'n toe Rev.E. o.Clleman,Miss Collin, Miss I .rwnoil, Mr. U. Perkins,the thildren,and all others who d v“oally or otherwise to the evening's ~r . iius. lie said tie derived the greatest satisfaction from the work of the Sunday schor.l in connection with Silver-street. He only wished they had the same accom- modation that. there was at Bold-street. It was a strong temptation to him to follow the question of education. In his financial duties be had a very full acquaintance with that particular question, but he dare not go into it then. It was a con- troversial question and he should not like to add any word that would give a feeling of inharrnonv to the meeting but he should like to say that in Warrington there was one iostitution which was one of the noblest in the kingdom and that was the People's College. It was one of the most perfect educational institutions ft young people of a certain class to be found. Warring- ton owed a good deal to it. (Applause.) We had nearly 10,000 children in attendance at our day schools and W 3 had not come into actual touch with the School Board, and perhaps Mr. Natkins was not far wrong when he said it was the 21. or 3d. in the £ that turned the scale. It was the strong desire on the part of certain clergy in Wnrrington. At that time he believed in them owing to the rate being 6s. 6i. in the £. Education did not stiffer much either at the hands of the managers of the schools or the authorities of the town. Referrine• to the curse of gaMbling the speaker said he had seen in the papors laudation of the result of the Derby (" Shame.") In an evening paper he read that at a meeting in a certain institution a vote of thanks had been passed to the Prince of Wales for winning the Derbv, and side by side with it he read of the suicide of a man owing to the same race. War, it or just that those who vrere at the head of affairs should take Dart in the gambling institutions of the day? (Cries of "No" and applause.) The Rev. G. D. MASON seconded the vote of thanks which was carried unanimously, and after Mr. Pigot had also been thanked for his services during the anni- versary, the meeting terminated.

div.head: SPEECHES ON THE EDUCATION QUESTION.
div.p: SPEECHES ON THE EDUCATION QUESTION.

In connection with the Sunday School Anniversary at Bold-street, Wesleyan Church, Warrington, a public meeting was held in the church on Monday evening. Mr. James Dodds, Lvmm, occupied the chair, and there were also present,the Revs. 0. Watkins,G. D. Mason, E.
o.Colemarl,tdr.W:Bitcuck and Councillor J. Shaw Green
'nem was -a fair attendance.
The CHAIRMAN said he came there with great pleasure on the invitation of Mr. Silcock, and he was largely influenced by the fact that he should meet once more an
old friend—Mr. Coleman—who though he was only in the circuit a short time won every heart in it by his tenderness, gentleness and loveable characteristics. He
took it that they were there that night in con- tinuance of the services :of Sunday which he believed were most successful, and devoted to the sus-

tenance of the Sunday school work in connection with the church. , He could only say that he hoped the anniversary might bo. financially and in other ways, the most successful of all. He thought that even in a meet-

ing of that kind they might be -reminded of the great conflict which was taking place in relation to the general educition of the people of the country. There were two points he would like to insist upon. The first was that we should take care that the standard of efficiency in . . _

the schools should not be lowered. (Applause.) Hobe. lieved there were working men present and he told them that upon that depended far more the progress of the country than upon many of the questions they were interested in. (Hear, hear.) Unless we saw that the people were well educated we could not as an industrial community and courtry hold our own in the markets of the world. He thou_ht further that as culture and edu.cation extended the greed of wealth would become reduced. (Hear, hear.) As people obtained more,educa- don there would come with the delight in culture a lessened desire to pose as the owners of money bags,and a greater desire for attaining to heights in culture and character. Education, he expected, would make all classes desire wealth less, and love the increase of culture to such an

extent that they would get the level that people wanted more readily than in any other way. The standard of efficiency should not be lowered, and in the second place no more assistance should be given to denomina- tional schools unless they were to be problicly controlled. (Hear, hear.) It was said that the conflict was between church and chapel. He was not going to say whether it was so or not, but he had looked up the his- tory of the thing to see which way such conflicts had gone.He was glad to And that in every crisis where English liberty had been fought for, the Dissenters, Methodists. and Nonconafornaists generally, had always been on the right side, whereas in almost every case the other side —without naming them—had been in favour of tyranny and the alliance of despothm, and the friends intellec- tual bondage. Mr. Dodds thought he had indicated pretty well what Noncomformists ought to aim at, and if we kept true to our celours he believed we should see—perhaps not this century—those same colours car- ried to victory because they were right,and not because they happened to be our colours. In Warrington, the speaker thought the question had been neglected, and he called upon them as Nonconformists to take their part in the discussion of the question. (Applause.) The Rev. o.Wkrxims said the burning question of the day was one of education. We were asleep in Warring- ton and the secret was that we were so terribly afraid of having new taxes that we played into the hands of anybody to save ourselves 2id. in the Z. (Hear, hear and applause.) We were so enraptured in having things on the cheap that we would let the Roman Catholics or anybody else sweep the board, and it was a disgrace to anybody connected with the town. (Applause.) He thought the duty of the State was to provide secular education for the children, and that every child born in England had a right to receive a good, sound, thorough, elementary education, which should put into his hands and head trech powers that if he would he might by his ownelndustry and application raise himself to a better position than that occupied by his fathers. (Applause.) Fie held that such an education must not be anti- Christian and that in our schools the Bible ought to be read. (Hear, hear.) He would like to pay what was very seldom paid, a just tribute to the noble work of the Christian day school masters, and mistresses, an achers, who rendered a magnificent service to State- by teaching the children in a Christian m. ner. (Applause.) While he held it was the duty of the State to provide education he held just as intensely that it was the duty of the Church to provide a spirituel education for every one of her children. He should look upon it asa great impertin- ence if a Roman Catholic priest or Church of England minister should COMA into his school—suppose he had one—and address the children belonging to it. It was a thing utterly alien to the spirit of a Christian State. The fight would be there. There was no question about that, and he wanted them to look it fairly in the face. He did not go to Silver-street to teach the children Methodism and he would be ashamed of himself if he did. It was a State-aided school and they had a noble schoolmaster. Clergymen and ministers had no business to bring their teaching into any State-aided school in the land,and when the State aided religion in that sense it was a bad thing for religion. (Applause,) He felt sure that in the future the Church which most carefully pro- vided for the religious education of the children would he the church of the future. (Hear, hen Nand applause.) He thought they understood the working of the 27th clause,and that a minister.or clergyman, or priest, could go into any school that was State-aided. He greatly de- plored that that might be the case. More than one could play at that game and he was confident that it would not be a spectacle tending to elevate, to find the vicar of Warrington in one corner of the school, the superintendent of the Methodist circuit in another, the Salvation Army captain in another, the Roman Catholic priest in another, and the Plymouth brother and a number of sisters at the door. If that sort of thing ever came to pass it would be a dis- grace to Christian religion (Hear, hear.) He was afraid that the Christian conscience had gone to sleep on the matter of responsibility to our own children. He admired a churchman because he stuck to his church. Roman Catholic in Warrington was a Roman Catholic everywhere, but a Methodist, sometimes, was all sorts of things according to the atmosphere of the places where he happened tobe. He would not expect a church- man to send his boy to Mr. Osborne's school at Col wyn Bay. because, although it was a grand school, the boys were under distinct Methodist influence and he would be ashamed of a churchman if he 'sent his boy there unleee he wished him 'to become a Methodist. They SS Methodists too must see that they sent their children to

a Methodist school. With regard to the ordinary rank and file of our children the Stindar schools of the future w;ould in a great measure be responsible as to whether we retained our young neonle or not and if our Sunday

schools were to fulfil this vaetly ine-reased application which the tenor of the time.; seemed to be thrusting upen them they would have to vaatly improve in diseip- line, modes of operation, and even in the character of a great deal of their teaching. (Applause.) The speaker way convinced more and more that we needed not only to train teachers in day schools but also in SundAy schools. (Hear, hear.) He did not need to argue that lessons in a Sunday schoel did not come to people by wishing for them and he need not tell Sunday school people that the be teacher, were those who prepared most carefully oy,et their classes. We needed to put into our child-en'e minds and hearts the truth as we held it. The Churches of England and Rome did that, and they were right, and Methodism would be wrong altogether until it did the same. (An- pleuse.) If we were to advance on the path of liberty and progress it would only be a. the reeult of being thankful to God for the privileges He hail given us. The only way for us to maintain and extend our liberty was by taking up the burden and seeing to it that no child left either home or Sunday school until he or she had a distinct,clear,and Heine, view of the troths of our faith. The fight on the Edeeatian Bill had been riehtlY.. defined by the Chairman a. a fight between priestism on' one side and liberty on the re her,or between church and chapel. Nonconformists wantel to take away no liberty or privilege from the Church of England or any other Church,but they claimed:equality in the face of God and man,and by God's help they would care for their chil- dren and seek to make them good citizens. (Applause.) The Rev.E.O.Cormax said one of the points brought up in the meeting was how to retain their elder scholars. They had solved that at Bold-street, and he used te rejoice in the number of grown up scholars of the Sunday school who'continued to attend. He thought the most in connection with that question depended very much upon the work that was done in the school while the scholars were young. (Hear, hear.) If they got the boys and girls converted to God they would not be in a hurry to run away. He fourd up and down that people were inventing all sorts of things ro keep the young people. There were P.S.A.'s, bicycle clubs, and tennis clubs which were all very well in their way. The great work of the Sunday school teacher, was, it seemed to him, to seek for the conversion of the scholars. The questions they had listened to that night were important and the remarks timely, but while our educational experts were s.ttling those matters their work in the Sunday school was definite enough. The speaker's experience, extending over a good number of years, was that thoae converted young stood quite as well as those converted in elder years. They must have converted teachers, and he thought that they could not lay too much stress upon it. Teachers should personally appeal to the scholars for their conversion to God, and they would see a great rn my brought to salvation. (Applause.) Mr. W. Smeocx said he believed Sunday school work was making progress, and that young men were begin- ning to realise the responeihilities of life. The hope of the Church, country, State, and world was wrapped up in our boys and girls. There were some people who depreciated youth and paid the young were apt to judge , in haste. The speaker believed in the young and instanced the triumphs of youth in the realms of war, art, science, poetry, music, etc.

div.head: MEN OF GREAT BRITAIN.
div.p: MEN OF GREAT BRITAIN.
THEIR WORDS ARE ABOVE REPROACH.
The interviews which follow are from people suffici. ently known, and the reader can be assured that every word they say is true.

They are certainly most remarkable assertions, and coming as they do just at the present time they can be read with the grettest interest and profit by all. Mr. %V. Hooking, Railway Inspecror, of Rochester, in response to an enquiry, said :—" For a long tirne I suf- fered from Liver complaint. I tried Warner's S ife Cure. from which I received great benefit after taking a few bottles."

Mr. S. Cross, of 44, Moor Crescent, Hunslet, Leeds, declared :—" I suffered for years from sluggish Liver, with frequent attacks of Jaundice, and was reduced almost to a skeleton. Doctors failed to do any goodibut Warner's Safe Cure restored me to psrlect health. I can now eat any kind of food and enjly it, and that is what I have not done for years." when in his speech this week at the Congress of Chatibers of Commerce of the Empire he practic- ally advocated a return to protection as a means of bringing about Imperial Federation. it is only necessary to point out in this connection that while in 1894 this country imported comm3dities worth 93 millions from the colonies, the imports from foreign countries amounted to no less than 314 millions. When bearing these figures in mind it is easy to realise the tremendous effect which an attempt to tax foreign goods would have upon the trade of this country. It is not surpris- ing, therefore, that the representatives of some of the most important Chambers of Commerce in Lancashire and Yorkshire protested against the resolution which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN commended, and that as a matter of fact this resolution was in the end not adopted. But still Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN'S speech will not readily be forgotten. It will show the country that the Liberal Unionist element in the Government can not be trusted to uphold free trade principles, and it will help to spread that growing distrust of our present rulers which was so plainly manifested in • the bye- elections of last week.

IN connection with the Mines Bill Death in the which is now before the House Mines. of Commons, it is mentioned that during the last forty-four years, no fewer than 48,219 miners have perished by violence. On the average, therefore, every year that passes sees the death by accidents of one kind or another,ef more than a thousand of the underground workers in this country. When it is said that, according to the opinions of many experts, a large portion of these deaths are due to preventible causes, the need for further protection of the miners will be admitted. During the period between 1851, and 1890, Lancashire heads the list in regard to the number of explosions which have caused the death of more than ten persons each. There have been thirty-two of these explosions in this county, and the number of killed was 1,399. Glamorgan- shire comes next with twenty-seven ex- plosions but this smaller number of ex- plosions caused the death of a larger numbers of persons, namely, 1532. On an aver- age fifty miners have been killed by each of the larger explosions. It is disappointing to learn that while in recent years the smaller acci ents have decreased in number the larger and more destruc- tive have shown no signs of diminution. It is still more disquieting to be told that the number of deaths for each explosion steadily increases. In 1851-60 the proportion was 2.98, but in 1891-4 it had risen to 9.04. The cause of most of the des- tructive explosions was at one time a puzzling mystery, but it seems to be now 'Pretty generally admitted that coal-dust is the most culpable agent. It is hardly necessary to ray that the friends of the miners in the House of Commons do not look upon the Bill of the present Government as all that it might be, but no doubt they will be prepared to accept it as an instalment. It should at all events do something towards preventing the death of 40,000 brave workers during the next forty years.

At a meeting of the District Council on Tuesday Mr. Heywood made a communication of consider- able importance to the ratepayers. It will be remembered that Mr. Heywood and Mr. Ashton,the clerk to the Council, have been in negotiation with the Ship Canal Company with a view to having certain clauses in the Bill now before Parliament made more fair to the Council, and Mr. Heywood on Tuesday seemed sanguine that the matter would be amicably eettled. It is encouraging to hear that there is a prospect of a long dispute coming to an end with the avoidance of the expense of litigation which will naturally ensue if the Council and the Manchester Ship Canal Company do not arrive at a settlement.

The goad resolution passed through the instru- mentality of Mr. Woodward at the last meeting of the Board of Guardians, deciding to send the girl out of the House to the board schools has brought about a peculiar deadlock. The Dutton Board School is at present quite full, and unless the build- ing is enlarged, the children of the Dutton Work- house can not be received. The School Board feel that they should not be expected to bear the whole cost of alterations, and they are looking forward to receiving assistance from the Guardians. Meanwhile the matter is roferred back to the sub-committee whose duty it will be to prop3und a sulutioa to what is beginning to be a knotty question.

COMING OF AGE REJOICINGS AT FRODSHAM. The workmen of the Scotland Bank Works of Messrs. N. Greening and Sons, Limited, were in- vited by Mr. and Mrs. Carter to a garden party at their home at Eversley, rodsham, in celebration of their son's (Mr. Gilbert G. Carter) attaining his majority, to which about 90 responded. The party were conveyed by 'busses starting at 2 p.m. from the werieta. On arrival at Eversley the party were received by Mr. and Mrs. Carter, and .conducted over the beautifully situated and well laid ont grounds and hot houses. The company were enter- tained to tea at the front of the louse, a eituation which commanded a very line view of the east and southerly portion of Cheshire. After tea, Mr. Wyllie proposed, and Mr: O'Brien seconded, that a hearty vote of thanks be given to Mr. and Mrs. Carter and to Mr. Gilbert G. Carter for the treat which had thus been given to the workmen of the company, and the hope was expressed that M.G. G. Carter might en- joy long life, and abundant success. The vote was heartily accorded. Mr. Carter replied by expressing the pleasure which it had given Mrs. Carter and himself in being thus able to give them all a few hours of enjoyment, and to see the kindly feeling entertained towards their son. Mr. Edward Woods then stepped forward and presented Mr. Gilbert G. , Carter with a beautiful gentleman's dressing case, ' as a small bur tangible token of their esteem, from his fellow workmen, on completing his apprentice- ship,• and attaining his majority. Mr. G. G. Carter replied. sincerely thanking them all for their many kindnesses and well-wishes. A photo of the whole party was .then taken, after which a musical treat was given in the commodious hall of the house, which was thoronghly appreciated. The company evidently set out with a full determination to fully enj▪ oy themselves, and every facility was given for them to do so. All will bear in memory their visit to Mr. Carter's at Proclaim= for some time to come.

RUNCORN AND THE SHIP CANAL.

On Tuesday the deputation appointed by the Runcorn District Council consisting of Messrs. P. Speakman,J.P., C.A., J. W. Lightburn, J.P., and G. Hewitt attended at Manchester. and interviewed the directors of the Man- chester Ship Canal Co. The business was the discus- sion of several matters including the granting of in- creased facilities to the town. The subjects were fully gone into, and the proceedings were of a very amicable character. The members of the deputation were not prepared to make the result of the meeting public until the negotiations have been successfully carried through.
FUNERAL OF A RUNCORN _TRADESMAN.

The remains of 'I homas Clough,butcher, of Regent-st., were interred on Wednesday afternoon in the Runcorn Cemetery. The service was conducted by the Rev. W. Scholes. In the carriages following the hearse were— Messrs. A. Healdley, J. Clough, W. Friar, A. Dutton, S. Dutton, S. Carr, J. Dutton, F. Daniels, R. Rolles, J. Stevens, F. Rooney, C. Watson, F. The coffin was of polished oak, with brass mountings supplied by Mr. Caygill who was the undertaker. Deceased was 28 years old.

div.head: RUNAWAY HORSE- AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A RUNAWAY HORSE- AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday afternoon a horse and cart, belonging to Mr. Samuel Claff, furniture dealer. Egerton-street, was standing near the shop. While the bit was being taken out of its mouth for feeding purposes the bridle slipped off ts head and the animal started off. Catterill, the man who was about to feed it made an attempt to stop it but he failed and was knocked known and con- siderable bruised. The horse went at full speed down Egerton-street and along Brindley-street, and ran against a blank wall in Blantyre-street, which brought it to a standstill, but not before the horse was severely injured about the kead and legs. A piece of furniture in the cart was also badly damaged. ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN BICYCLIST.

Dlr. William Bunt, of Carzon-st., Runcorn met with a serious accident while cycling near Winnington Park, Northwich. He was riding along the channel to avoid a newly set piece of macadam, when his machine came into contact with the curb stone and he was thrown violently to the ground. Mr. Hunt received very severe bruises, and one of his ribs was injured. He has been under the care of Dr. McLennan,and the progress he has made is considered satisfactory. At the same spot half an hour before the accident to Mr. Hunt, a Manchester cyclist was thrown and had his arm broken. THE VEHICULAR BRIDGE QUESTION.

On Thursday a meeting of the Highways and buildings Committee of the Runcorn Urban oDuisieterict of tCf idopurnocvilwinags held in the Town Hall, and the a b a bridge across the Mersey for vehicular traffic between the two counties was introduced. It was thought that the matter was one for the consideration of the Parliamentary and General !Purposes Committee and it may confidently be anticipated that at an early date the preparation of a scheme for constructing such a bridge, will be taken in hand. The advantages to be derived by Runcorn and Widnes from this connection between the two prices, cannot be over estimated, and if the local authorities can bring the matter which has long been before the public to a successful termination, it will be a subject for congratulation to the two towns con- cerned.

div.head: GHOST LAYING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: GHOST LAYING AT RUNCORN.
A NIGHT IN A." HAUNTED " HOUSE.

The ghost story which has been going-th-e—rOunds in Runcorn excited considerable interest during last week end and the beginning of this week but practically the matter has now gone be- yond the three days' wonder stage. During the week several offers were made by would-be ghost hunters but permission was reserved to the representative of the " Examiner" and a few friends to spend the night in the haunted chamber." Tuesday night was selected for the visit and at about 11 o'clock our representative joined a* party comprising six members, at the street corner. At that time the street was perfectly ' quiet and ingress to the premises was easily oh- , tabled. The house is a four-roomed building erected on modern lines and it certainly does not look either ghostly or uncanny. Beyond the fact of its being empty there is nothing to single it out ..from any other - house in the street. On getting inside, the back room or kitchen was speedily taken possession of by the party, and arrangements were made for the passing of the vigil in comparative comfort. One member produced from his pocket two or three candles which, on being stuck upon the mantleboard by the primitive process of melting one end of the candle and trusting to the setting of the wax to hold it upright, lit up the room in a creditable manner. Seats were formed out of the cupboard drawers, and draughts were prevented by neatly pinning a newspaper over the window. Having made everything as comfortable as possible the members of the party after declaring themselves ready for the ghost or any other unearthly visitant, began to cast about for means to pass the time until daybreak. Ghost yarns and cards found the chief favour, particularly the former, told by an elderly gentleman with a view to depressing the spirits and ardour of the amateur ghost layers. Between a 1.30 ancl 12.30 a visit was paid by a well-known medical man, who having failed to frighten the ghost hun- toss by masquerading with the folds of a borrowed sneet, got in the house and made himself sociable with the rest ot the watchers. By that time all expectations of ghostly visits had been abandoned by the inmat•is of the house, and the only question ptta'arstytehgaedt tthhee ettilmsteexopneeptieletaisoannotlfys.eeiN of the ngone anything uncanny, but there was a feeling that some noises caused by natural means had been the secret of the propagation of the ghost story. During tbe night, however, not the vestige et a sound was heard,save those made by the watchers tnemselves,and beyond 'the domes little joke no apparitiona were seen. A few facts may be mectioned which may have a tendency to clear the matter up. In the middle of the house is a door which when not closed swings zomewhat heavily on its hinges and makes a creak- dug noise which would he easily magnified by nerv- •ous people into semething that should not be. At the rear of the house is a stable and during the night the horses were heaad to stamp their feet and this may account for the sound of footsteps coin- 11,plained of by. a tenant. Acother little thing,which, though a trifle in itself, may account forthe appari- ' Lion, may be mentioned. When the back premises are lit up and the doors joining the front and back zooms together, are open, a peculiar refection of the light is thrown upon the front window. This resection is in turn thrown on a window across the road, and the effect produced by walking across the front room in the dark is that of suddenly seeing a sheet of light. As this can only be seen ire one pesit,ion it might have an unpleasant effect upon a nervous tenant, though at the same time the cause aisd the effect can be easily seen by walking across the room These little incidents which have been mentioned are of course plainly accounted for on natueal grounds and nothing ghostly can be attri- buted to them, and beyond than nothing whatever was heard in the house on Taesday night. div.head: OUTSIDE SCHOOLING.
div.p: OUTSIDE SCHOOLING.

Mr. Charles E. Dutton, clerk to the Dutton School Board, wrote as follows under the date of June Bth, 1896. --.1 Your letters of the 13th and 27th ult, were read at a meeting of the Dutton School Board on Saturday last, when after discussing the proposal of the Guardians the following resolution was unanimously passed. On the motion of the vice-chairman (Rev. L. D. Lyon Bennett) seconded by Mr. Fowles," while fully sympathising with the proposal to send the children from the workhouse to outside schools, and believing that such a course would greatly benefit the children, the Board School is limited to an average attendance of 60, and at the present the average attendance is 57, and that therefore there is no available accommodation for the children from the work- house." I was further directed to state that before the children could be admitted it would be necessary to pro- vide additional accommodation and teaching staff, and that the coat of this should be borne by the Guardians in accordance with clause 24 of the Bill now before Par- liament, which runs as follows :—" The Guardians of any Unimn. may contribute towards such of the expenses of providing, enlarging, or maintaining any public elementary school as were certified by the Education Department to have been incurred wholly, or partly, in respect of scholars taught at the school, who are either resident in the workhouse or in any institution to which they have been sent by the Guardians from a workhouse or boarded out be the Guardians."— The Clerk reported that Messrs. Woodward, Baxter and Heywood, tagether with the Clerk (Mr. Ashton) waited upon Mr. C. E. Linaker on Friday. the sth inst., and explained the wish of the Board to send the girls at once and the boys in the near future to the Dutton Board Schools, when Mr. Linaker explained that at the present time there was accommodation for 60 children, and that 56 were on the books, but these included chil- dren who resided outside the township of Dutton. If these latter children were excluded there might be seats for 10 er 12 of the children but if more than that num- ber were sent more school accommodation and an extra teacher would be required which, of course, could not be provided except at considerable expense. That if the Board of Guardians could see their way to assist the School Board in defraying the expense be apprehended no difficulty with his Board. But if on the other hand the Guardians could no; see their way,. he was afraid they would not willingly accept such children. In the course of discussion it was suggested that the Clerk to the Guardians should write to the Local Government Board and ascertain whether the Guardians would be permitted to contribute towards the expense of provid- ing the additional accommidation at the. schoola and .towards the expense of an additional teaching staff, and It was also suggested that Mr. Lien Sher should ascertain front the Dareebttry School Board at their irzt meeting whether they would accept the infant children at their Preston Old Hill School.—Mr. Woodward moved that the report and Mr. Dutton's letter be referred to the cub. committee appointed for the purpose. In the meantime there would be one difficulty as there were some children in the house who were not attending school, and he would like to ask the master how many infants they had. —The Master stated that there were nine infants—Mr. Woodward continuing said that g ould make 20 elder children. They were in the position that the Board School had 56 children,lo or 12 of which were not resident in the district. They had contributed to the rates in support of the schools, and he thought they had a clear claim on the Dutton School Board, but at the same time it was their duty to contribute to every extra exit incurred by the School Board. The difficulty was what would they do with the children in the meantime P—Mr.Talbot said the question had been asked Mr. Kynnersley the school inspector, if they could prevent outside children coming to the school, and he told them they bad no such power. —Mr. Woodward believed that though Mr. Kyonersley might be correct he thought that the schools had to have a certain number, and the Board could fill up the vacant places.—Mr. Talbot said the school would have to be enlarged if the children of the workhouse were taken, and he thought it would be hard on them if they bad to bear the entire expense they would he put to.— The Master pointed out that a number had pissed the fourth standard and might stop in the house for an in- dustrial training.—Dr. Gastaldi seconded the raotion.— Mr. Hey wood opposed the motion and proposed as an amendment that they advertise for a teacher and keep on the industrial trainer. He approved that the matter should be referred to the committee, but did not think in the meanwhile they ought to follow Mr. Woodward's suggestion, that the children should be sent to the schools in the :neantime. He did not want tc come to any public contest wi,h the School Board of Duttontand he thought the matter would be better deferred until the time was more ripe for the removal of the children.— Mr. Aaron seconded the amendment,and Mr. Talbot sup- ported. On the question being put to a vote six voted for and 12 ags inss the amendment. This brought the business to a close.

RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUnIL.

The fortnightly meeting of this Council was held on Tuesday at Dutton Workhouse, when there were present Messrs. J. Mclntyre (chairman), H. Talbot, J.P., T. Baxttr, C.C., J. Knowles, J. Stokes, J. A letter was read from the clerk of the Cheshire County Council stating that the provisional order as to declaring certain highways in the Nortlawich and Run- corn Rural District Council had been confirmed, and wiring when the amounts agreed upon would be paid over so that instructions could be given to the County Surveyor to take over the maintainance and repair of such highways. div.head: ALLEGED NUISANCE AT FRODSHAItt.
div.p: THE ALLEGED NUISANCE AT FRODSHAItt.

Mr. C. E. Linnaker, of Frodsham,writing on the above subject, wished to be informed if it was the intention of the council to do anything further in the matter. The nuisance still existed and had not been abated in the slightest degree. The stench was abominable and the swarm of flies was enormous. If the council came to the conclusion that they could not move further in the matter he should be compelled to take steps to protect himself. Be war exceedingly sorry that this was neces- sary as he had no wish to interfere with any trad. or the employment on any labour but the Railway Company should be compiled to provide for traffic of this excep- tional description,special accommodation.—Mr. Wright moved that a copy of the letter be sent to the Railway Company.—Mr. Talbot seconded, and said he was down there the other day and there were blue-bottles flying about in millions. (Laughter.)
MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

Dr. Adams reported that three fresh cases of typhus fever had occurred at Sea Villas, Halton,and one case of typhoid fever at Frocisham and Aston. There had been four scarlet fever outbreaks at Stockton Heath, one at Halton,one at Lower Walton,one at Aston, and three at Preston Brook. A ease of diphtheria had been notified from Dutton and there had been a slight outbreak uf measles at Overton.

RUNCORN AND THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY. With-reference to the Ship Canal Bill Mr. Heywood gave the result of the meeting which took place between himself and Mr. Ashton from Runcorn and representa- tives of the Manchester Ship Canal Corn3any. They at- tended on Tuesday last and met the engineer and solici- tor of the company and they arrived at a very satisfac- tory arrangement providing the directors agreed with it. By the Friday morning following Mr. Ashton re- ceived the directors mutilation of the clauses which practically amounted to getting nothing they wanted. He and Mr. Ashton went on Saturday last and again saw the engineer and the solicitor and again arrived at a satisfactory arrangement providing they got the ap- proval of the directors which had not yet come to hand. The company was in a deal better frame of mind than what it was in the House of Commons and would be glad to settle,and he was looking forward to an amicable settlement withoet retaining counsel or anyone. Mr. Ashton however thought that it would be better to have the Bill watched through the House of Lords because other authorities might object. Mr. Aaron proposed that Mr. Ashton and Mr. Hey- wood attend in London for that purpose,and Mr. Wood- ward seconded the resolution which was carried.
This was all the business of public importance.

div.head: COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTION AT RUNCORN.

On Saturday polling for the vacant seat on the County Council lately filled by Mr. P. Speakman on behalf of the ratepayers of the south division of Runcorn began in earnest. The candidates Mr. A. R. Norman, and Mr. E. Imison together with their supporters were early in the field, to secure the polling of the votes promised to them during the week. Mr. Norman during the week, addressed many meetings and elected to fight the con- test as a Liberal, both politically and from the new ed- ucational point of view. On the other hand Mr. Inaison sought the support of the electors as an iadependant and in his train he carried with him as supporters several prominent Liberals. On the register were 977 voters, and for the polling convenience of this number, two stations were decided upon situated in Victoria-road Board Schools. In No. 1 booth, Mr. G. F. Ashton was the presiding officer with Mr. Harry Wright as poll clerk while in No. 2, Mr. Frank Johnson presided with Mr. W. Flough,'as poll clerk. The hours of polling were from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.and as the afternoon wore away the two parties made every effort to bring voters to the poll. The election literature was not extensive,though voters were asked per placard to "Vote for Norman, and justice to every denomination." " Vote for Norman, the Liberal Candidate," and "Liberals be true; Vote for Norman." Immediately after the closing of the poll a crowd assembled in the vicinity of the Board'Schools. Count- ing operations were expeditiously carried out under the supervision of the returning officer,who was able shortly before nine to declare the state of the poll to be
Mr. E. Irnisoo 425 Mr. A.ll. Norman 377
Majority
The nevrs was received with cheers by Mr. Imisou's fol- lowers.
SPEECHES HT THE CANDIDATES.

Mr. Imison. C.C., addressed those assembled from his committee room steps,and said that during the progress of the'slection it had been stated that lithe battle was gained by him it would be d,oicribed as a Tory victory. It would be unfair to those Liberal friends of his who had so loyally supported him if he were to make any such claim, and the first notion he wished to repudiate was that it was to be regarded in any such sense. (Cheers.) The next denunciation he wished to make was that it as not a Church victory over Nonconformity. (Applause.) That would also be unfair to his Noncon- formist friends, who had so earnestly assisted him in the contest. (Applause.) He was not quite sure whether he could regard it as a victory at all, but rather a pro- test of the electors of the south division of Runcorn against the introduction of politics into the matter. (Cheers.) He thought there had been an object lt-ssou taught in that respect at the time the District Council was formed, and he certainly thought so far as County Council elections were concerned, there there never was a politician returned as such, but on independent lines like those adopted by him. In that respect he considered the electors had proved themselves eminently wise. (applause.) If a man had to merely look after the interests of a party, he was not the member to re- present the welfare and advantages of the whole of his constituents. (Cheers.) That was the notion he should carry into the County Council, and he believed every elector would accept the assurance that party lines sh-uld be his last consideration. (Applause.) His opponent had invariably shown him the greatest pos- sible courtesy,and his supporters had treated him almost in the same way, and therefore he asked them to regard that as not a victory over Mr. Norman, but a victory over the principles he had for the time represented. (Cheers.) He hoped his conduct oo tho County Council svould give them satisfaction. If at any time he acted contrary to their expectations, he ventured to entertain the opinion that they would net send him again. He, however, believed it was possible to work those matters apart from politics, and the result showed that the elec- tors shared the same views. Ho begged to thank them , for the good feeling which had been displayed, and which he hoped would be long continued ; for the way in which they supported him; and in return he assured them that he would serve them faithfully and well. (Cheers.) Mr. Norman, whose committee room was next door, also addressed the crowd. He had been defeated,anel as he said in the room where the counting of the votes had taken place, he gave everybody credit for having acted according to their convictions. (Applause.) The great point was that every man had a right to his opinion, and his was the great question of politics. Ile centended that politics could not be kept out of the County Council. (Applause, and a voice : " Yes, they can.") He should not. have mentioned that only for Mr. Liaison having just introduced it, and he felt that he must say that his convictions were that it was impossi- ble for a man to pocket his politics, and it was impossi- ble to act without them on the County Council. The issue had been placed before the electors. He had acted according to the best of his ability, and he endorsed all the kindly remarks of Mr. loaisan. lie had tried to act in a straightforward manner, and to avoid personalities or hitter feeling. When he commenced that contest lie had a hearty shake of the hand of his opponent, and at the close the friendly relations were not more strained than whenl they began. (Applause.) He hoped that was the feeling of the electors. Let there be no bitter- ness,but let them look at the event as one in which they acted according to their convictions. It only remained for him to thank those voters who had supported him that day. He thought, without going particularly into matters.he might say that he had been handicapped,and taLing evers tiong into consideration he had made a good fight, for be had received only 48 votes less than cue of the most popular men in the town, who had been sup- ported by many of his(the speaker's)own side in politics. (Applause.) Mr. Speakman said he had during the contest received provocation from the other aide, but he had not replied, becaUse what had been said was from belief of their point of view. For 71, years he served them well, and according to his ability in the Counts' Council, anti therefore the members of that body had shown that they appreciated his services. He was about the first to con- gratulate Mr. Itnison upon the dignity that had been conferred upon him that day, and it would be his plea- sure to help him in the Council. He hoped the bitter- ness, if there was any left, would from that moment Pass away, and that the only thought they would have was that Runcorn should prosper in the future. (Applause.)
l'he crowd very shortly afterwards dispersed.

div.head: DARESBURY PARISEI NURSE
div.p: DARESBURY PARISEI NURSE
ASSOCIATION.
ANNUAL MEE LING.

The annual meeting of the above Association was held in the Sessions-room, Daresbury, on Saturday ev3ning, amongst those present being—Mrs. Rodgers Miss Dutton> Mrs. Killington, Mrs. C. Baguley, Mrs. Webb, Mrs. Wil- son, Mrs. J. Fairclough, Mrs. C. Do Prez, Mrs. Gulick, Mrs. Houghton, Messrs. G. Rodger, T. Billington, J. Taylor, J. Ryder, J. Houghton, J. Prince, Mrs.. Rodger took the chair.
SECRETARY'S REPORT.

Before presenting the yearly report Miss Dutton (hon. secretary) read several letters of ap ,logy for non-atten- dance,including one from Lady Brooke, who wished the association every success, and acknowledged the able services renderei by the nurse to Mary Dearn,of Norton —enclosing a subscripion of oneguinea. The following replrt was then read :—Tue committee are glad they can present a report of a most succecsful year. Never before have so many parishioners availcu them- selves of the services of the nurse. S...ee she entered upon her duties in July las: she had attended 231 cases, and has made such a number of visits that they would be difficult to estim- ate. Analysed these cases are as follows : Accidents. 16; bronchitis, 14 ; scarlet fever in the earliest stages, 18 ; fractures, two ; wounds, uicers, &c., 15 ; children's dis- orders, 38 ; confinement cases, eight; kidney disease, two; influenza, eight ; abscess, eight ; phthisis, three ; bums and scalds, five ; sunstroke, one ; neuralgia, two; diarace t, ten ; skin diseases, two ; dyspepsia, nine ; throat complaints, six ; inflammation, four • &c. In several urgent cases Nurse Allen has attended her pati- ents throughout the whole night, and during several consecutive nights. Many chronic patients have had her services throughout the year at frequent intervals. She has attended professionally many operations, by appointment with the doctors who have highly appreci- ated her services. Several medical men have expressed their high opinion of the -value of her assistance, and subsequent attention and skill, which have secured so completely the carrying out of their orders. In a few prolonged and most critical illnessess this has been con. sidered the almost indispensable means in securinc recovery. A new feature in the work has been the mid— wifery branch of it, where Nurse Allen's skill has been a valuable adjunct. _

Nurse Allen has been the medium through which in. many cases the needs of sufferers have been made known and relieved, and she has beetkindefatigable in carrying out with ,much discretion the work of supplying very needy patients with nourishment and warm clothing.. Never has the work been so fully appreciated by the parishioners generally, and the largely increased num- - tier of subscribers must be taken as one proof of this. The committee conclude their report hi expressing their very grateful recognition of the nurse's Liaoning devotion to the interest of the patients of the association."
TREASURER'S REPORT.

The Treasurer (Mr. Rodger) gave a report of the finances of the association, and after referring to the seccession from the subscribers' rank about a year ago, which represented a loss of about £7O, he considered the parishioners had responded well, as they had only a defiAt of £l5. This sum had already been made good by the guarantors. At present about one fourth of the families in the parith were subscribers, and another year others would be asked who would undoubtedly assist in the gool work being carried on. The names of subscri- bers and amounts were then read out by the Treasurer, showing a total of £63 184. 10i. for the year. It was decided that the secretary's report and balance sheet be adopted, printed and circulated throughout the parish.

OFFICERS AND COMMITTEE. It was also carried that the treasurer and secretary be re-elected for the ensuing year ; and also the following Ladies' Committee rt-Aected with power to add to their number :—Mesdames Rodger,Baguley,Littlemore,Billin,g- ton, Congreve, Johnson, Webb, and Miss Dutton. Miss Dutton then proposed that the best thanks of the meeting be given to Mr. and Mrs. Phillips for the use of the room.
This was seconded by Mr.Billington and carried unani- mously.

Mr:Rod:ter. proposed that a hearty vote of thanks be given to Miss Dutton for the deep interest she had always taken in the work of the Association, and with her per- mission he would couple with her name the name of Nurse Allea for the excellent way she was fulfilling her duties
This was seconded and carried with acclamation. Miss Dutton thanked those present for the vote of thanks, and assured them that the work bad becn a pleasure to her.

div.head: REMARKABLE LIBERAL VICTORY AT' A SCaOOL BOARD ELECTION.
div.p: REMARKABLE LIBERAL VICTORY AT' A SCaOOL BOARD ELECTION.

A notabte Liberal and Nonconformist victory has just been achieved at Flo!beach, South Lincoluahire,where a School Board election has taken place under similar cir- cumstances. In February a new Board was elected without an appeal being made to the ratepayers. More than the requisite number of candidates were nomin- ated,but the returning officer,Mr. R. P. Mossop,solicitor, rejected five of the nomination papers on the ground of intormality, and all of these ,;nolidates were Liberals and Nonconformists. This resaaed in legal action being taken bv Mr. Robert Merry, leader of the Liberal and Nmconiortnist party in the town, one of the rejected candidates, who petitioned against the return of the members. The petition was heard before Baron Pollock, , and was successful, and the Board was accordingly did- solved. The sequel was a fresh election, ,irdered by the Education I.)-partment. Fourteen candidates went to the poll ft the seven seats. Through the rejection of nomiaation papers on the ground of informality. too Jectors of nolbeach had had no opportunity of exercis- ing the franchise at a School Board election for a period of nine years. The rusult shows that the, p9lititcal and religious complexion of the Board has undergone a re- markable transformation. The new Board consists of five Liberals and two Conservatives, against six Conser- vatives and one Liberal previously ; whilst there are tour Nonconformists and three Churchmett, as compared with aeve.n Churchmen on the old M.:rd. Four old members have berm defeated,ineuding two clergymen The result of the election is a signifi'..,sot victory for :riibera!isin and Nonconformity.—" Daily iNiesvi."

Norman, nuisance inspector, prosecuted, and the necessary evidence was given by Inspector Powell. A SAVAGE ASSAULT.—Johh Lee, Turner-strePt. and Mary Bridge, Rodney-street. were charged with assaulting and beating Sarah Ann Sutton on the 30th May—Bridge pleaded guilty and Lee not guilty.—Mr.P Davies prosecuted and said that the attack commenced at 7 o'clock on Saturday night. Mrs. Sutton was then goinr home and met Mary Bridge at the bottom of Rodney-at. Defendant was drunk and rushed at complainant and struck her in the mouth. Complainant went in her own house.but between 9 and 10 o'clock she came out again and defendant again rushed at her and dragged her into Lee's yard, where she shouted to Lee Come on Jack and punch her brains out." Lee then came out and kicked her on the right temple. She was black and blue all over, as another woman had joined in and kicked her. Complainant had been under the care of the Infirnatt,y doctors ever since. —Mrs. Sutton corroborated this statement with regard to de•endants.—Further evidence was given by Mary Cartledge. —Evidence for the offence did not disprove the charge against Mary Bridge.—Mary Bridge was given a months' hard tabour and Lee was discharged, there being no evidence against him._

-AN INTER-FAMILY SQUABBLE.— Joseph Ward, 1, Buckley's- yard. was charged with assaulting Maria Ward, 5, Bakehouse. yard, on the 30th May.—Maria Ward, defendant's sister-in- law, said defendant struck her in the month.—& girl corroborated and defendant was sentenced to a month's hard labour.—Cornellus Ward, brother of last-named defendant, was charged with assaulting Mary Ward on the same date.— Complainant stated defendant had knocked her down and had ki,...ked her —Phcebe Queenie supported complainant's statement and defendant was fined ss. including costs. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. J. Burgess. THE MAN WITH THE ELECTRIC BATTERY.—Robert Fair- hurst was brought up on remand, charged with being found in possession of an electric battery, supposed to have been stolen.—The Chief Constable said that it was true that defendant bad bought the machine. Apparently he had the idea of making money by it at the sea-side, as he was in possession of several railway excur.ion bills to sea-side resorts. —The defendant was discharged. 31IONDAY,—Before the Mayor (chairman), Aldermen Wright and Francomb. and Messrs. div.head: SHORT TALK ON BEING-
div.p: A SHORT TALK ON BEING-
TIRED.

.1' ARE you a.. working man, or a working woman? I don't mean one Who is so by classification, or by having been born on the sinister side of certain lines of social cleavage, but solely because you daily do some sort of ::banest; and useful work? Yes ? I shake your hand. :I hope you manage to live by it without over doing, and that (being still hearty and healthy) ynu sometimes find yourself tired, dog-tired, and hungry as a wolf, witirplenty of good feed for supper. Then hey! tor bed and a genuine sleep of eight hours; to jump from bed in the morning, both feet on the floor at once. '?bat's the right kind of" tired" and the heaven des- tended brand of rest. It is a blessing in itself, and bears others in its train.

But the variety of fatigue so many people are all the time writing us about is different. Listen to this one, for instance: "In September, 1393," he says, "I was overcome by a feeling of languor. I was easily tired and comparatively slight efforts served to exhaust me com- pletely. Indeed I never seemed rested at all, and was as tired in the morning as when I went to bed. Both muscles and mind were inert and relaxed. At the same time my appetite seemed to be tired too. I had no re- lish for food, An d after eating felt uneasiness and dis- tress in the stomach and pain at the chest. My skin was sallow also, and there was a dull aching at my right side in the region of the liver.

"I was constantly belching up a sour fluid, and my food would sometimes ' repeat ' or rise into my mouth. All I could do to rectify this miserable state of things I did, acting upon the suggestion of friends and others. but failed to come acr,sl a remedy for my complaint, which meantime obtained a stronger hold upnn me.

"On account of my bability to eat and digest food my flesh fell off until I became so thin you might have fancied mo as having gone into a decline. And I was so weak I could scarcely get about. I remained in this condition month after month, unfit,'of course, for work and virtually a man out of the world's fight. "The doctor who prescribed for. me probably under- stood my case, tut he was not able, apparently, to cure me. And I notice it is in illness as in business ; unless one holds his own he is bound to be falling behind which made me anxious to 01-tain relief soon, lest I might pass beyond the reach of it. And in answer to the hope finally canae the help I needed, " In July of last year (1894) I read about Mother Seigel's Syrup in a small pamphlet which was left at our house. The book described my symptoms, perfectly ,and stated the disease to be indigestion, with dulness and inactivity of the liver, the latter condition a result of the former. The weakness and loss of weight it ex- plained,' naturally enough, to be the effect of want of proper nourishment. Cure the stomach troubles in such cases, said an article in the pamphlet, and the conse- quences will vanish of themselves. "On this I procured a bottle of the Syrup from Messrs. Robinson and Co., chemists, Hunslet Carr, and after taking it for a few days, I found myself much better. My food now ceased to give me pain, and I gained aims strength with every meal. No better proof of the power of this medicine could I ask. I continued the use of it; the bad symp- toms abated and no longer troubled me, and in a few weeks I felt as vigorous and well as ever I did. I could work as before and experienced that kind of fatigue which promotes rest and is relieved by it. I have since enjoyed good health, and you are welcome to publish this short account of my case. (Signed) Percy Hard- aker, 42, Woodhouse Hill-road, Hunslet Carr, Leeds, March 29th, 1895."

Mr. Hardaker is agent for the Pearl Assurance Society, and is well and widely known. His own intelligent comments on his complaint renders any words of ours quite needless. In private conversation he said he looked upon that unnatural" tired" feeling as a warn- ing that none should neglect. It means, not the effect of work,but of exhaustion through the subtle disease in- digestion. Mother Seigel's Syrup should be taken then, as he would have taken it then had he heard of it. We hope Mr. Hardaker's timely words, based as they are on an instructive experience, will be heeded by all to whom they apply.

SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CRICKET CLUB —OPEN- ING OF NEW GROUND.—OR Saturday the ground of the above club.aejoining the residenre of Mr. Brough, "The Poplars," Lovely-lane, and kindly placed at the disposal of the club by that gentleman, was orened by a match with the Windsor Wesleyan C.C., Liverpool. A large number of spectators witnessed the game, including a good many ladies and gentlemen from Liv•rpool. The first ball was sent down by Mr. Browili, the pre(ident of the club. The visitors hatted first, hut could do very little against the excellent bowling of Liewell, and Watkins. who took 4 wickets for 12, and 5 for 11' respec- tively, Bullen being the only man to reach double figures (18) all the side being out for; 44. On the home team going in to bat runs were put on raridly, the visi- tor,' total being passed with 6 wickets in hand. F. Taylor 26, C. Llewellyn Maria Sudlow 11, played a good game. The total reached 91 leaving the home team easy winners of a very enjoyable game. In the evening the visitors and teams adjourned to th. Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Schnol.where a splendid tea was provided and to which full justice was done.A social evening was after- wards spent, presided over by the 11,0,v. W. (1. Triggs. Amongst others there were present the Rev. P.J. Byrne, Councillor Tinnion, Mr. J. W. Hayward, J.P., Mr. Z. Bradburn, Captain Savage, Mr. Brough.ancl others. The following ladies and gentlemen contributed largely to the Success of the meeting. by their musical abilities, Miss Taylor. Miss H. Brom+, Miss BraFiburn. Liverpool ; Mr. P. L. Richardson, Mr. S. Bradburn, and Mr. T. Broug.l2 proved themselves efficient accompan- rapists. A very pleasant evening was brought to a close by a vote of thanks. Scores :

A BROTHERS' QUARREL AT BOLTON.—k tragic affair occurred on Tuesday night at Wellington Yard, Corpor- ation Depat,at Bolton.An engineer engaged there named John Davies, was visited by a brother named Robert, who continually tramps the country. Suddenly the men began to quarrel, and when the workmen rushed to separate them, it was found that Robert had a fearful gash in his throat, and that John had a knife in his hand. The wounded man was removed to the infirm- ary, where he lies in a critical condition, and John was taken into custody. The magistrates; were sent for to take the dispositions of the injured man, who, however, may recover.

div.p: NOTES AND NEWS.

At the Electrical Exhibition at New York, on of the novel features. according.to the "Electrician," was the transmission of the roar of Niagara by telephone. The sound was gathered near the Cave of the Winds, where a wooden box some 3ft. square was placed on a rocky ledge, and inside this a telephone with " solid back" transmitter t 3 which latter was fixed a sheet-iron funnel 14in. in diameter and 201 n. long. Three batteries were placed in the box, but only two were used. By this means, the roar, as heard in the world-famed Cave of the Winds, was electrically transmitted to New York,a distance of 462 miles. At the same exhibition some in- teresting feats in telegraphy were shown to vast audien- cies, messages being sent round the world and received back within a very short time after their despatch. In one case a message sent via London on -to Tokio and back to New York, by a 'route covering in all 27,000 miles was received back in New York in about fifty minutes. Another message sent all round South America was returned in twenty-three minutes.

Of the Boer witnesses who have come to this country, one of the most interesting is Lieutenant Eloff, the grandson of President Kruger. As will be remembered, it was the young lieutenant who went out to meet Dr. Jameson and was disarmed. Mr. Eloff pere was at one time private secretary to his father-in-law, the Pr,sid- ent. The son entered the public service, and is now a lieutenant in the police,. being stationed at Krugersdorp. Mr. Piet Grobler, a grand-nephew of President Kruger's, is returning to South Africa in a few days from the visit he has been paying here. Mr. Grobler,who speaks English admirably, has made an excellent impression here for good sense and ability.

A correspondent of a London newspaper *rites :—I have not noticed in the English papers the result of th. late Referendum on the education question in South Australia. The result was a three to one majority in favour ot the continuance of the existing sybtem of State education ; a two to one inakuity against the introduc- tion of scriptural instruction; and a four to one majority against any payment being made td denominational schools for secular results. It is clear that Australia is as completely prepared as the United States has been found to be in recent years to adhere to a single system of public elementary schools.

In the aptitude for putting political points in homely and effective metaphors, President Kruger is almost as good as Prince Bismarck. Who will ever forget his comparison of the tritlander movement,before Dr. Jame- son's raid,to a tortoise? If you want to kill it, said the President,you must wait until it puts its head quite out. And now, when he has released his prisoners, he is re- ported to have used another metaphor, not a whit less effective. "If my little dogs are naughty," he said, in replying to the thanks of the released prisoners. " I must. whip them, but lam always sorry to do so. Next time I must get bold of the big dog. My little dogs bark, but the big one bites." What could be better in its way than that. Some other of the President's reported savings are al=o very good. "Each hand,he said to An interviewer who was doing an unoffi;ial "deal " wizb him some years ago, •'must wash the other. If one hand washes and the other does nothing, one hand remains dirty. That will not do." The Boer case against the Uitlanders. again, has never been so well put as in some of the President's metaphors and pointed sayings. The Uitlanders,it was urged. bring money into the country. "True," replied Mr. Kruger, " but what for? In charity or as a present? No! They bring a lot in to fetch a lot out." "Why should I let the llitlanders in to political privileges ?" asked the President. " Before water of which you know nothing is admitted to mix with pure water you subject it to a long process of puri- fication and distilling." "Give us the whip and reins." say the I:titian/len ; "our stock, our property is also in the cart." " I admit that,"repliei the President. " Our belongings are in the same cart. But where are you go. in to drive me to? And how do I know that you don't mean to upset me."

The correspondent of the " Chronicle " at Brussels writes :—Official figures having been recently quoted to 'hew that the number of horses imported last year from Eeeland exceeds 22,000, instead of 8,000, as stated in the Belgian Chamber. I visited Antwerp with the object of finding out approximately Y hat proportion of this enormous total! is actually slaughtered for human con- sumption. From information courteously placed at my disposal by the director of the city abattoirs, it appears that the hulk of the animals arriving from England find their way direct to the slaughter-house. Although the greater Part come from Londonsthe trade is by no means confined to this qnarter, the imports in last week'', official list showing that no less than 48 were brought from Roll and Newcastle. One dealer in Antwerp alone (an Englishman) disposed of upwards of 3,000 horses last year to the local butchers. On the other hand it is positively denied, as far as Antwerp is concerned, that any of the meat finds its way back to England, either in the form of" tinned beef" or soup. Not a single meat- preserving establishment exists in the city. My inform- ant, who is a staunch adherent of horseflesh as a s. wholesome and nutritious diet for the working man, confirmed the measures about to be taken for gusrding against tuberculosis and glanders. A further experi- ment is about to be tried at Rotterdam by subjecting all "suspicions "meat to treatment in steam chambers heated to .11.0 degrees centigrade (a temperature which has been scientifically proved sufficient to kill the bacillus), and to sell the meat so steamed at prices rang- , ing from if. 50c. per kilo. (about Bd. per lb.), the resi4ue of the broth included. There are in Antwerp about thirty shops devoted entirely to the sale of horseflesh. I visited several of these establishments ; but With the thermometer at 80 in the shade, the meat, of which the bulk had been slaughtered at least two days previously, did sot present an appearance which was calculated to make converts. Still less so were the sausages of dusky hue, which appear to form the staple delicacy when the meat is unfitted for sale in its natural state. The prices run from 40. per lb. for" prime cuts "to about 21. for "scraps.". When it is remembered that, anart from the Government ban laid upon imported horseflesh, there is In Belgium a duty of nearly U. per lb. en all other imported meat, it is easy to understand why Australian mutton is yet practically unknown here, and why among the poorer classes horse is the only flesh food available.

A telegram from Metz of Tuesday's date states that two members of a party of thirteen British officers, who had arrived there in order to visit the battlefields of the Franco-Prusqian War, went up the Cathedral tower on Tuesday morning, and when at the top made s.me sketches. The military telephonic post stationed in the tower, observing what they were doing, at once in- formed the Town Commandant, and the two officers were arrested. They were conveyed from the guard- house to the chief police office, where Maser Sim had no difficulty in proving that the arrests were due to a mis- understanding. Both officers were liberated at noon.

On ;Tully 1, we are likely to see a new development for Great Britain in the matter of express trains. The three East Coast Comnanies (Great Northern, north Eastern. and North British) are about to not on their road a train equal to the best American " Palace Car" expresses in the character of its vehicles. while keeping the compart- ment divisions in each coach which is thought to he so dear to the English heart. The compartments,however, will be neither" stuffy nor "lonesome "—certainly not the latter, as they will all either open into a corridor, or (in some of the 3rds) have a central passage through them ; the height of the " clerestory "roofs, and the immense" gauge" width—about 8 feet 6 inches—will effectually keep them cool in summer ; in winter they can be heated to any temperature required by steam from the engine. The two special features of the trails, which will mark it off from any as vet run in this island, will be (1) the" Gould " vestibules, joining each coach to the next one by a central passage, with the " Gould "self-acting coupler. instead of the usual screw chains and hooks; (2) the fact that each vehicle will run on twelve wheels (a six-wheeled bogie truck carrying each end of the coach). The former arrangement enables the largest train to round sharp curves with per- fect safety, while the latter will ensure beautifully smooth running at any speed.

The awful tornado which nearly destroyed St. Louis is no longer a mystery. Professor E. Stone Waging, of Ottawa, has given the following conclusive and lumin- ous explanation of the phenomenon :7-These cyclones had the same cause as that which partially demolished Louisville, Ky.. on March 29, 1890; namely, the lunar conjunction with the sun. The moon was in perigee and in conjunction on the 28th, and, occurring at nine hours west of London, had the maximum of power in forcing the atmosphere over the Atlantic westward against the Rocky Mountain chain. This increased the force of the current that runs up the Mississippi Valley and down the Great Lakes. At such conjunctions the earth is slightly compressed and electricity fills the at- mosphere, which immediately begiße to absorb mils- tnre. The atmosphere, when not electrically charged, is perfectly dry and cannot hold water in solution. The particles of air composing the atmosphere then repel each other and the air Fs light. This Mississippi current was then under great electric tension and was loaded with vapor. Suddenly the telegraph wires converging in St. Louis, which stretch in all directions ever the vast areas of the West, beeiu to draw off the electric force from the current. The air particles, being no longer held asunder, rushed together and an air column over the city in a moment became heavy and sank down to- wards the city, and the surrornding air, rushing in to fill the void, created a cyclone, just as a sinking ship causes a whirlpool. That's the thing in a nutshell.

Mr. A. N. Hornby. of Nantwich, acting on behalf of the Cheshire Hunt Committee, has offered a reward of £2O for information which will lead to the conviction of the Person or persons responsible for the killing of foxes in the South Cheshire country. In all about 14 foxes have been destroyed. A valuable staghound and two sheepdogs were also found dead in the same district re- cently. The stomachs of several dead foxes have been sent for analysis, and the police have the matter in hand.
