The officials of the British Mediterranean Squadron were entertained at Rome on Thursday. Six hundred icketS ot the squadron will visit Rome on Sunday. Of this number 400 are Irish Catholics, who will visit the Vatican, and attend Mass to be celebrated by the Pope in the ?auline

At the Central Criminal Court on Wednesday, Charles Milsom surrendered to his bail and pleaded guilty to committing perjury in the course of proceedings in- stituted by him for a divorce. The defendant was land- lord of the Royal Oak Inn, near Chesterfield,and ita April last year he obtained a decree nisi agains'-, his wife, but the Queen's Proctor subsequently successfully intervened on the ground that the defendant had misconducted himself with a young woman who was staying at the inn, and who had a child. The defendant, in the divorce proceedings, anied the misconduct.—Mr. Mathews, in mitigation of punishment. urged that the defendant had been actuated thoroughout by a desire to marry the young woman and act honourably by her.—Mr. Justice Hawkins sentenced the prisoner to three month's im- prisonment.

The Board then proceeded to consider the appointment of successors to Mr. and Mrs. H. M. Mines, as superin- tendent and matron of Ridgate Industrial Schools. The advertisement stipulated that " The persons to be appointed must bc‘ husband and wife, salary as superin- tendent £3O, as schoolneaster £5O, matron £25, with apartments, rations, etc. If the superintendent is com- petent to undertake the duties of bindinaster, an addi- tional sum of £lO per annum will be granted." The DEPUTY CLERK informed the members that at the meeting Df the CDmmittee on Tuesiay in the previous week, when 32 applications were considered, rtriking 84 in all, it was decided to lay three names before the Board, and the following were selected :—Mr. and Mrs. Allen, Newland, Hamstead, Birmingham; Mr. and Mrs. Cann, of Orford Sc,ools, Warrington; and Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Wright, Union Schools, Birkenhead. _ _ _

After a little discussion it was decided to consider the applications in the alphabetical order given. The testi- monials of Mr. and Mrs. Allen were than read. From them it appeared that Mr. Allen was 27 years of age and Mrs. Allen 26 years. Both were members of the Church of England, and had resided in Warrington. On being called into V- e room, they were questioned by the Chair- man and other members of the Board. Mr. Allen said he had had no experience in poor-law schools. He had not been to Padgate Schools, having only arrived from Birmingham the previous night. He had had no ex- perience in keeping books for Union schools but he did not think he would have any difficulty in that respect. Mrs. Allen said she had had experience in cooking and dressmaking. She held a Government certificate for dressmaking. She had not been a school teacher.—The Chairman said it was not so much a schoolmistress that was wanted as a general manager, one, for instance,like Mrs. Ward at the Workhouse.

Mr. and Mrs. Cann's testimonials were then read. They were both members of the Church of England and were each 42 years of age. On being called into the room, Mrs. CANN said she had visited thet;schools.—Mr. CANN sail( he had never had any experience in Poor Law scholls, but he had heard of the duties that would be required of him, and he had no hesitation in saying that he would be able to do the work. He was organist and ehoirmaster,but he had not conducted a band. They tad three children and they would like to have the children with them if possible. Mrs. Cann was an experienced cook and had conducted cookery classes witi success at People's College.—Mr. MINES said Mrs. Cann had given lessons in cookeryat the schools. _ _

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.
NORTHERN RUGBY UNION.
DRAFT SCHEME OF MANAGEMENT FOR 1596-7.

'The Northern Union is at present busily engaged in setting itsitiouse in order for the forthcoming season ,and a series of meetings has been held by a sub-committee charged with the duty of drafting a scheme of manage- ment for the ensuing season. Three of these meetings have already been held, the third taking place at Brad- ford on Monday evening. No official details were giv9n, but we understand that the constitution of the two county competitions for next year has already been settled. Sixteen dabs will form that for Yorkshire, which will consist of the eleven which formed the York- shire Section of the Northern Union for last season, with ' the addition of Leeds Parish Chtirch,Castleford,Bramley, Heckmondwike, and Holbeck. The title of the competi- tion, it is suggested. thould be the Y.rkshire League. The Lancashire SeJion will consist of 14 clubs, and will be entitled the Lancashire League. The bylaws and rules of the game, we understand, hav€ also been under review, but in these two respects no important changes are contemplated. The sub-committee have also for- mulated the scheme for the Northern Union Challenge Cup. This will be on the principle of the division of gates up to the final and semi-final rounds. when the Union will take one-third of the gate after expenses have been deducted, and the remaining two thirds will be divided between the cont-sting clubs. A further meeting of the sub-committce has to be held before the whole scheme is submitted to the governing body, and this will piobably take place at Manchester. There it is in contemplation to propose the constitution of county committees—one each for Yorkshire, Lancashire, and Cheshire.

div.head: ALLEGED SWINDLING AT
div.p: THE ALLEGED SWINDLING AT
WA.ItItINGTON.

Before the magistrates at the Warringt:.-ai Borough Court on Monday, John Grant, the ex-Warrington furniture dealer, appeared to further- answer the charge against him. Mr. Browne said that a receiving order in bankruptcy had now been made against prisoner and information had also been laid 'against him for obtaining £6O on false pretences. It would be impossible to go into the case that morning, as the Quarter SPssions commenced the morning after and the Official Receiver also wanted to see the prisoner the same day to prepare the usual statement of affairs. He therefore applied for a remand until Saturday. Mr. F. R. Roberts said if Mr. Browne would assure him that the case would be gone into on Saturday be had no objection. Mr. Browne nromised this, and prisoner was then re- manded until io-day.

div.head: NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.
div.p: NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.
GARRET RONAYNE.—We cannot re-open the case in these columns. SURSIIM CORDA.—Received. JOHN MARTIN.—LibeHOUS.
WiLuAm GILL, M.l.J.—The matter is one in which we do not feel called upon to interfere, even in the way of a " journalistic courtesy."
THE ILLNESS OF THE REV J. YONGE.

Sir,—Will you permit me thus to offer you my very sincerely grateful acknowledgment of the many kindly references in your columns ta my recent illness ? And may I also, through you, convey to the large number of friends, representing all creeds, sects, and parties in Warrington, who made sympathetic enquiries, my deep sense of their great kindness ? It has been exceeding gratifying to me to discover that, not only my friends at Wycliffe, but my fellow townsmen generally, hold me in a cordial esteem which I shall do my best to cherish and retain as long as I continue in Christian service in their midst. I may add that it is my hope to resume active duty early in July. —Yours faithfully, JOHN YONGE.
Bryn Celyn, Llanfairfeehan.. June 4, 1896.

div.head: BETTING AND GAMBLING.
div.p: BETTING AND GAMBLING.
SERMON BY TFIE REV. E. T. REED.

There was a good attendance at the Emmanuel Re- formed Church, Warrington, on Sunday evening, when the pastor, the Rev. E. T. Reed preached a special ser- mon on" betting and gambling," taking as his text "If the foundations be destroyed what can the righteous do." Psalm xi. 3. After some introductory remarks the preacher said that the workingmen of this country because of their predominence in numbers might rightly be regarded as the foundation of the country,and it was of the utmost importance that that foundation should be preserved from those who would destroy it. There were, un- happily, intermixed with workingmen of England those who ministered to their vices and who by means of allurements and temptations were breaking down the moral stamina of the race. Amongst those allurements and temptations betting and gambling were amongst the very worst,and the extent to which they were now being carried on by the working classes throughout the country • was simply appalling, and called for the earnest opposition of every Christian, every patriot, and every philanthropist. After giv- ing definitions of gambling as understood by authorities on the subject the rev, gentleman went on to say that gambling to him stood in precisely the same relation to stealing that duelling stood to murder. Every gambler was really a thief whether he stole 3d. or £l,OOO. Be obtained without effort and without merit thet to which under the circumstances he had no claims whatever. Every gambler should be branded, whether in private houses, on the Stock Exchange, or at a bazaar, as a thief, and they would have stabbed gamb- ling at the heart. Referring individually to outstanding features in alliance with the evil the preacher said that according to Whittaker's Almanac there were no less than 122 racing fixtures during the present season, extending from March 23rd to November 28-,h and occupying no less than 261 days. There seemed to him no reason why horse-racing legitimately pursued should not be as harmless as any other athletic sport, but as a matter of fact horse-racing gathered round it the very worst and demoralised elements of the population. The jockeys, he said, were mere stable boys who were apprenticed to horse-trainers and by them taught to ride. There was as a rule nothing athletic about their appear- ance as they had to be small and light of weight. Most of them were uneducated and yet what heroes they became to the betting and gambling fraternity. Some years ago inland revenue officials assessed the gains of one jockey at £9,000 a year and another paid income tax on £lO,OOO a year, a sum equal to the salary of the Lord Chancellor of England. An honest working- man earned perhaps his £2 for 6 days honest , toil and an uneducated jockey tnight receive I £l,OOO for riding the winner in a great race. Those were the men who were regarded as heroes by thousands. Could there be any greater absurdity? Betting had now its own organized system. It had been estimated that there were from 10.000 to 15.000 profeseianal book- makers in this country, men who did nothing to produce wealth or to promote the well-being of the community, but, on the contrary, men who lived upon the hard earn- ings of their dupes, the working classes. These and Ulric assistants were daily plying their accursed trade in every town. There were almost as many bookmakers and their agents engaged in their dishonest and immoral trade as there were teachers of religion and morality. They flecked to every race meeting, every football match, cycling competition, athletic sports, coursing meetings, and other similar gatherings. Their object was to get those who attended to invest their money in the form of bets, which was highly immoral, and, therefore, most injurious to charact.r. On the other hand the object of ministers of religion, school- masters, teachers, &c., was to inculcate morality, self-control and to stimulate men to that which wa; noble, good and pure. The absolute folly of betting and gambling, he said, was nowhere more easily see n than in the blind faith which many young men placed in the sporting prophets and tipsters who for a consideration were. prepared to give advice to those who were foolish enough to fall into their snares. Mr. Reed instanced from facts the incor- rectness of many of these eporting " tips." He observed that se long as the leading newspapers gave their sanction to the great evil of betting and gambling by publishing betting and racing news, it would be impossible to do much to check it. In Warrington the vice was undoubtedly very prevalent Some private and public places had attained great notoriety by the wae in which the evil had been carried on. All classes, and especially the working classes,were affected by it. It was strongly entrenched in the work- shops, in the public thoroughfares it had been carried on under the very eyes of the police, and up to a very recent date their efforts to check the evil had been some- what hindered by the absence of any bye-law prr hibit- ing street betting. At the last meeting of the Town Council, however, on the recommendation of the Watch Committee, a bye-law was paseed rendering it illegal for any person or his agent to frequent or use any street or other public place within the borough for the pur- pose of bookmaking or betting or wagering or agreeing to bet or wager, under a penalty not exceeding £5. The last time he had occasion to allude to the Town Council was to call attention to what he believed was a step In the wrong direction, namely, the sanctioning of Sunday concerts in Parr Hall, and, therefore, it gave him all the greater pleasure to draw attention to whet was un- doubtedly an important step in the right directien, and one which he hoped, would be the means of checking the growing evil. The Town Council, the Watch Com- mittee, and the Chief Constable, and police in enforcing this new bye-law would have the support of all right- minded people in the town, and when eases came before the magistrates it was to be hoped that they would sup- port the police in their difficult work. When Arpley Meadows came within the boiough, it was also to be hoped that the pitching and tossing which was carried ' on there would be put down with a firm hand. The preacher concluded by imploring young men to have nothing to do with betting or eamblin instancing the sad end of many gamblers Only by their abstention from it could the foundations of our national life be preserved from injury, and as a nation should we be enabled to fulfil the great purpose which was marked out for us by God.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1896.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1896.
WARRINGTOS WORKING NIEN'S PER- MANENT BENEFIT BUILDING SOCIETY.

There was a good attendance at the annual general meeting of members of the ,Warrington Workingmen's Permanent Benefit Building Society, held in Gulborne-at. schoolroom on Monday evening for the purpose of elect- hg managers, auditors, and surveyors, and conducting the ordinary business of the s:ociety. Amongst those present were : Messrs. John Hatton, C. B. Haines,James Hardin, E. Wallington.E,lward Fenton, R. Isherwood, J. W. Bouchier, J. Baxter, S. Burdett, William Bodle, William Charnock. G. Corlett, James Colledge, W. H. Wallington, J. Mills, E. England, Wilding, W. Win- stanley, Greenough,Edwardson, Evans, flayes,J.Potter, and Josiah Longland .(solicitor to the society), and P. Dalton (secretary). On the proposition of Mr. FENTO!T, seconded by Mr. ROBERT ISIIERWOOD, Mr. John Hatton was voted to the chair.

The CHAIRMAN congratulated the members on the successful year they had had, and stated that taking, everything into consideration, the accounts were satis- factory. They were not,however,in a position to pay a dividend this year, and perhaps on that matter some ex- planation would be necessary. The SECRETARY then read the annual report and bal- ance sheet. It stated that during the year, the sum of £1,309 153. 11d, had been received as subscriptions; £2,625 16s. M., for repayments ; and £27 43. 2d. en- trance fees, fines, etc., making the total receipts, £3,962 16s. 7d. The working expenses were £73 63. 91. The withdrawals amounted to £929 17:3. 31. The sum of £3,550 had been advanced to members. There were 222 subscribers holding 296 shares and 41 borrowers holding 191* shares, making 263 members holding 487 i shares. The Onuses amounted to £621 las. on the amount lent. Under the Building Societies' Act, 1894, the accounts of all billing societies are required to be made up in such a form, and to contain such particulars as the Chief Reeis'rar of Friendly Societies may, with the approval of the Secretary of State, direct. The form of account which has been prescribed by the chief registrar requires that the balance of capital remaining due upon the mort- gage should be stated separately from the prospective interest thereon, in other words the balance of the £B2 103. (the net amount advanced per £100) remaining uneaid is to be di .tinguished from the balance of the £l7 103. (the bore s charged) also remaining unpaid. The accounts of the Society for the pest year have been made up on this basis and work out as follows :-Total amount remainine owing upon mortgages £11,116 93.61. of which only £9,901 63. Bd. can be regarded as capital, the balance of £1,215 33. 10d. representing the propor- tionate amount of interest thereon, calculated for the number of years the several mortgages have still to run. Although the Society started the year with reserve and contingent funds amounting to £645 Bs. 2d. yet nearly the whole of the balance (after deducting working ex- penses) of the amount charged by way of benus upon loans during the past year is required to increase these funds to a sum equal to the amount of the prospective interest as stated:above. It must, however, be born in mind that this state of affairs does not arise from the society having sustained any loss during the past year, nor from its being in a less flotirishing condition than hitherto, but solely from the fact that instead of treating the bonuses upon advances as profit for the particular year in which the advances are made, the bonuses are spread over the entire number of years which the several mortgages have to run. This alteration in the .method of dealing with the accounts, as will be seen from the foregoing figures,pre- vents the payment of ally diyidend to unadvanced members for the past year,but the managers confidently draw attention to the fact that, after providing for the payment of the full amount owing to unadvanced mem- bers amounting to £10,274 us. 24. the accounts of the society show a surplus on the mortgage securities and cash in bank equal to about 11± per cent, thereon, in the shape of prospective interest, a proportion of which, together with a proportion of the bonuses received upon advances made during the year will be available towards a dividend for the current year. The managers have used the utmost care in respect of the properties upon which advances have been made and they believe that there is ample security in every case. The whole of the managers retire, Messrs. Harding, Wallington, Fenton, Isherwood, Bouchier and Baxter. are eligible and offer themselves for re-election. Six additional managers will be taken from the register in rotation."-Messrs. E. Bradshaw, A.C.A.. and Samuel Albinson certified that the accounts and statements were correct. Mr. GREENOUGH thought some statement should be made explaining the reason why there was no dividend this year. Mr.l3orcatea (one of the managers) said it was rather an unfortunate position for the managers to be placed in when they had to bring before the members a statement of accounts that did not include any interest to be paid to the shareholders. But he thought they should regard the accounts as though they were the same as previous years. They would see that the bonuses for the year amounted to £621 10s. in addition to profits made from other sources which would have enabled them to pay 4 per cent, dividend and put something like £2OO to the reserve fund it they had dealt with it as before. The Chief Registrar said that the form they had adopted was not in accordance with law which stated that all mortgages should be treated in a certain way. The report and balance sheet which was presented that night made it quite plain. When a person purchased £lOO the society did not actually pay him £lOO but only £B2 103.' and the sum of £lOO had to be repaid at the rate of 4s. 11. per week. There was charged £l7 104. bonus per £lOO which was spread over a period of 9. years. The Registrar therefore said that the society had no right to call the money borrowed £lOO 'but only £B2 10s. plus the interest. They had always taken • the mortgage at £lOO because the mortgage was really the repayment and the person who borrowed had to repay £lOO. In consequence of their having to treat the accounts by the new rule, the whole of the reserve fund and balance had been swallowed up by the reduc- tion of the account for the arrears upon the mortgage securities. Thus instead of the amount remaining upon mortgages being put at £11,11695. 61., they new stood at £9,901 64. 84. This meant that the society had to provide £6OO in addition to the £645; they had as re- serve and contingent funds. With regard to next' year, he thought the society stood a very good chance of be- ing able to pay a very fair dividend. Next year, with- out reckoning what they might have from bonuses,there would be something like £3OO that they could take from the prospective interest fund in addition to anything the society might be able to make during the year. If they advanced £3,000 during the year,the society would be entitled to add the first year's Interest to the revenue, which was £3 4s. per £lOO. Re did not think it would be right to make the statement as to what the rate of dividend would be next year. The new requirements put the society in the position that if they dissolved to- day they could pay 20s. in the £ to every investor, ' and right up to the end they could pay interest,less any little expenses,until the winding up. (Hear, hear.) He thought under the circumstances there ought not to be difficulty in passing the accounts. They were in the unfortunate position of paying no dividendthis year. but they would be able to pay a dividend next year. What- ever the amount was next year, the one the year after would be greater because the interest would be greater. In answer to a question as to whether the Warrington Permanent Benefit Building Society would be compelled to make the same alteration, air.Boucutna said that the Society did not charge bonuses but interest year by year. That Society had no prospective interest to take into consideration,but they had. He might add that the managers had had a great deal of anxiety about the new Act, and they thought possibly the Registrar might he brought to look at it in a different light. He(the speaker) and Mr. Longland went to London and interviewed the Registrar,but it was quite impossible to move him at all. They pointed out to hint that the shareholders were chiefly workingmen,and were expecting some return on the year's working. The Registrar,however,considered that if the facts were placed before the members, they as reasonable men would see the advantage of the new Act and agree with it. Mr. EDWARDSON asked whether the dividend which had been lost to the shareholders this year would form an increment which would recoup the loss in future years. Mr. FENTON said as a manager and shareholder it was his opinion that if the members would be patient they would get the interest which they had lost this year. The cash was in the society and it only wanted time to divide it according to law. It was only saving the money. It was a disappointment to himself and perhaps to others that the usual dividend of 4 per cent, could not be paid, but they were obliged to adapt themsAves to law. He moved that the report and balance sheet be adopted. Mr. GREELEY hoped everyone would get a chance of speaking on the matter. Mr. R. Isnenwoou said he felt perfectly satisfie i with the statement that had been made. He did not think they had really lost their interest, and he was of the opinion that their dividends would be more satisfactory than in the past. He seconded the adoption of the report. Mr. WILDING said if they had to create a new reserve fund this year's interest was lost to the present share- holders. Mr. LONGIAND said with reference to the question of this year's interest, the Registrar told them that they could not eat their cake and have it too. (Laughter.) There was no doubt that in the early years of the society very large dividends were paid. Mr. HARDING : We have paid as high as 8 per cent. Mr. LONGLAND (continuing) said he did not participate in such dividends, as he was net then connected with the society,but if the members had been satisfied to pay the moderate dividends which had been paid during the past few years the present position of affairs would not have happened, because they would have had such a re- serve fund in hand that they would have been able to meet the present claim of the Registrar-General, and have set aside the prospective interest. Although they might have an increased dividend in future years, he did not think that that would be the case next year. He did not mean to say that next year they would have 8 per cent. Out of every £lOO advanced between the Ist of May this year and the 30th April next yearthey would be entitled to take £3 Is. per cent.lifor the)year's

div.head: EARLESTOWN A.ND NEWTON,
div.p: EARLESTOWN A.ND NEWTON,
GOOD TEMPLARY.-EBENEZER LODGE.

The Earlestown Ebenezer Lodge held its weekly Session on Tuesday evening in the Co-operative Hall. Bro. T. Dean, C.T. presided. The Secretary read the digest of No. /, Convention Session to be held at Hindley on the 20th inst. The Lodge de- cidei to commence open-air mission work. All the members were invited to visit Widnes on Saturday the .13tti inst., to take part in the Lifeboat Demonstration. The programme of the evening was then given, namely, " Wines : British and Foreign "the secretary being responsible. All the members took :part, after which the lodge closed. EARLESTOWN WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.

The annual picnic in connection with the above association took place on Saturday afternoon to Micklehead Green, the field and schoolroom there being placed at their dispo4ai by Mr. and Mrs. G. W. Rawlins. The party numbering about 80 left Earlestown in wagonettes about 1.30, a few going by train, Micklehead Green being reached about an hour later. Rambles in the country were enjoyed, and various games were indulged in until about 5 o'clock when tea was served in the schoolroom. Supper was served at 8 o'clock, and at 9 o'clock the return journey was commenced,horne being reached about 10 o'clock, after a most enjoyable outing. The arrangements were satisfactorily carried out by Miss Ashcroft (secretary), assisted by the committee.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARY.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARY.

The usual weekly session of the lope of Earles- town lodge of Good Templars was held in the Co- operative Hall on Monday evening. Bro. G. Clarke presided, and there was a good attendance of mem- bers and.visitors frem Ashton Excelsior lodge, who were heartily welcomed. The digest of business for No. 1 Convention was read by Bro. Nicholson, sec- retary, and adopted. Bro. B. G. Jones, of Widnes, spoke of a lifeboat procession and gala to be held on Saturday at Widnes, and gave a hearty invita- tion to the lodge to be present. Greetings from Widnes lodge were accepted and reciprocated, and all the members were urged to go to Widnes on Saturday next to take part in the lifeboat demons- tration. The Ashton visitors were then introduced and took various offices. Bro. J. Speakman, C.T. presided. Songs,readings,recitations,and dialogues were given by Bros.Jacksou,Bowler,James,Jenkins, W. llulme, Smith ; Sisters Smith, Blinstone, and Bowler. Thanks to the visitors for visit and enter- tainment were accorded, on the motion of Bro.War- burton, seconded by Bro. Parker.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE CLUB ANNUAL MEETING.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE CLUB ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual general meeting of the members of the Newton Polling District Conservative Club was held on Monday evening in the Billiard room of the Conservative Club, Earlestown. There was a good attendance, and Mr. T. J. Gillespie, J.P.,presided. Amongst those present were M.lssrs.C. B. F. Borron, C.C., J.P., W. Collingwood, W. ti. Owen,J. Catherall, T. Foster, T. Haselden (sec.), and others. The Secre- tary read the minutes of the last meeting, and also the annual report and balance sheet which were of a satisfactory nature. These were adopted and on the motion of Mr. Catherall, seconded hy Mr. J. Smith, Mr. T. J. Gillespie was re-elected president. The chairman suitably acknowledged the compli- ment. Mr. J. W. Thorpe was re-elected treasurer, and in proposing the re-election of Mr. T. Haselden as secretary, the chairman alluded to that gentle- man in very complimentary terms, remarking that the club owed a debt of gratitude to Mr. Haselden for the thoroughly efficient and business-like man- mer in which he carried out everything he under- took. Mr. Catherall seconded, and the , proposition was carried unanimously. Mr. Haselden responded and said that as long as he was secretary, his best endeavours would be made in the interests of the club. The election of committee followed, and this was composed of Messrs. G. Jones, T. Siddeley, J. Catherall,W. A. Mawdsley,J. Howe J. B. Owbridge, J. Smith, J. Kynaston. W. Moses, W. Parkinson, G. Wright, H. Littler, W. Sutton, W. Pierpoint, J. Hughes, and E. Layland. A vote of thanks to the chairman brought. the meeting to a close.

div.head: EAALFSTOWN ASSOCIA.TION FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: EAALFSTOWN ASSOCIA.TION FOOTBALL CLUB.

The annual general meeting of the members of the Earlestown Football Club was held at the Griffin Hotel, Earlestown,on Tuesday evening. Mr. T. Siddeley pre- sided and there was a fair attendance of members. The notice convening the meeting having been read the Secretary (Mr. J. Waddington) read the minutes of the last general meeting, which were confirmed on the motion of Mr. C. Lee. The financial statement which was submitted showed the receipts including a balance, brought forward from last year of £1 7s. 10d. was £256 94., and the expenditure including £lll 5. 7d. for players' wages and expenses amounted to £253 17s. 4d. leaving a balance of £2 us. 81. to be carried forward. On the motion of Mr. H. Thorp, seconded by Mr. J. Ogden, the accounts were passed. The Secretary said that at the present time thanks to the generosity of Mr. Pardey,the club was clear of ground rent, and for the future their ground rent would be £5 per year instead of £lo,and in addition to that the club was straight on Mr. Pardey's books. (Hear, hear.)—The election of officers was then proceeded with. Mr. James Horridge was elected treasurer, Mr. Thomas Hamer president, and Mr. Joseph Waddington was re-elected secretary. The Secretary, speaking with regard to the club's performance last season, stated the only results worth taking any notice of were the Allianoe fixtures, showing that they had played 22 Alliance matches, won 15, lost 1, drawn 6 ; scored 69 goals to 16 against, making a total of 36 points. (Hear, hear.) Messrs. Reade and Porter were appointed auditors. The following were elected to serve as a Committee :—H. Pritchard (52), J. H. Alderson (46), J. Jackson (46), J. Ogden (41), H. Crowther (39), J. Tyrer (38), 1. Topping (34), W. Mullins (33), J. Dearden (31), James Shaw (31), T. Sid- deley (29), L. Bullock (29). A vote of thanks was passed on the motion of Mr. J. H. Alderson, seconded by Mr. H. Pritchard, to Mr. J. E. Pardey for his kindness and generosity in making such a substantial abatement in the ground rent for the field, A vote of thanks to tbe Chairman terminated the meeting.

div.head: DR. JAMESON'S TRIAL.
div.p: DR. JAMESON'S TRIAL.

The Police Court proceedings against Dr. Jameson and his officers are at length approaching a close. On Thins- day,when the hearing of the case was resumed,evidence was given by Lieutenant Eloff, a grandson of President Kruger, who encountered the raiding column soon after it left Mafeking, and was taken prisonf.r. Afterwards, he said, Dr. Jameson sent a message to the Boers that if he were resisted at Krugersdorp he wouldshell the town. A more important witness was Mr. Albert Fleishack,who gave formal proof of the discovery of a large number of letteis, t'Agraml, and plans in a couple of boxe3 which Dr. J,imeson had with him when he surrendered. The Attorney General read the principal letters, with the ob- ject of throwing light upon the origin of the raid and the parts which various persons took in it.
profits. As to creating a new resfrve fund, they would not have to create one. They had already got one, and that would increase as the business of the society in- creased.

Mr. EDWARDSON nail he had the fulltst confidence in the managers. He gathered one main point, and that was that practically the interest was gone this year. (Laughter.) Mr. LONGLAND said he was now speaking as a share- holder. He had been brought into contact with the managers,however, as sclicitor to the Society during the meetings that had been held to consider the position of affairs, and he could unhesitatingly say that they were desirous that the shareholders should have every infor- mation that it was possible to give. They had no desire to keep anything back. MT. W. H. WALLINGTON : Was it an absolute require- ment on the part of the Registrar that the accounts should be made up this year? Mr. LONGLAND replied in the affirmative. Mr. GREELEY said he was quite satisfied with the Society ; he considered it quite safe. Mr.Enweno WALLINGTON : The deputation to London forgot to mention one thing, and that was that the Re- gistrar complimented them on the flourishing state of the Society, and said that they were in a most enviable position. (Hear, hear.) The motion was then agreed to unanimously. RE-APPOINTMENT OF MANAGERS, &C.

Meslrs.James Harding,E.Wallington, Edward Fenton, Robert Isherwood,J. W. Bouchier, and J.Baxter were re- appointed managers ; Messrs. J. E. Wright and William Bodle, jun., surveyors, and Messrs. Samuel Albinson and Edw!n Bradshaw. A.C.A.. auditors. A vote of thanks to Mr. Hatton for presiding was passed, on the motion of Mr. ISHERWOOD, seconded by Mr. GREELEY.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. THURSDAY.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. THURSDAY.

In the House of Commons on Thursday Sir W. BAR- COURT asked the Colonial Secretary what was at present the official position of Mr. Rhodes in the territory of the British South African Company ; whether he was em- powered to control and reverse the action of Earl Grey as Administrator, whether he acted as managing direc- tor of the Company under a power of attorney which authorised him to do all acts and exercise all authority in like manner as if done by the Company, and whether the principal authority in the civil administration of the territory was at present legally vested in Mr. Rhodes. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN replied that Mr. Rhodes had for some years acted as managing director of the Company, and held a power of attorney substantially in the terms of the question. He (Mr. Chamberlain) was advised, how- ever, that the Company could not delegate to a manag- ing director or an attorney the power of reversing or controlling the action of the Administrator, and that consequently Mr. Rhodes had no power to con- trol or reverse the action ot Earl Grey. The principal authority in the civil administration of the territory of the Chartered Company was not, therefore, regally vested in Mr. Rhodes. Mr. P. STANHOPE asked the Colonial Secretary whether in order to avoid further bloodshed, he would instruct Sir F. Carrington to enter into negotiations with the " rebels "now concentrated in the Matoppo mountains, in order, if possible, to effect a peaceful settlement before any further military operations in the nature of rept i4als were entered upon. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said the information before him would not justify him in taking the course suggested. He would make it his care to see that considerations of humanity were not lost sight of so far as was consistent with the sup,ressiosi of the rebel- lion, the punishment )f the murderers, and the preven- tion of a recurrence of the present trouble. _ _ _

Sir H. VINCENT asked Mr. Balfour if he could SPO his way to translate the sympathy frequently expressed by him, on behalf of the Government, in favour of the Importation of Prison-made Goods Bill into action by enabling it to be brought forward. Mr. BALFOUR replied, tkat the prospects of public business had not improved since last he answered a question on this subject,and he could not now give a more favourable reply. On the order of the day relating to the Education Bill, the Speaker ruled out of order thirteen instructions to the committee standing in the names of different mem- bers. Oh the House going into committee on the bill, Mr. W. Allen moved to postpone clause 1 (which directs that "every county council shall appoint an education committee for the purpose of this Act "), and said thae if that was carried he should move to postpone tht second and third clauses, in order that the committee might at once get to the consideration of the special aid grant. Sir J. Gorst replied' that in the opinion of the Government the first clause was the most important in the bill. Mr. Dillon said the declaration of the Vice President would carry dismay throughout the country among the supporters of denominational schools. Mr. ASQUITH said the statement was,to say the least,un- expected. It was not possible.to discuss the composition of the new authority until they knew what its functions would be and bow the money it would control would be distributed. The motion was rejected,,after further dis cussion, by 262 votes to 121. The first three and a half pages of amendments were then declared out of order for various reasons by the Chairman (Mr.J.W.Lowther); and Mr. Luttrell moved that the controllipg educational authority should be the District and not the County Council. The amendment was rejected by 298 votes to 125. Sir A. Ronk proposed that the election of the education committees should be placed in the hands of the county and municipal boroughs After some discussion, Mr. A. J. BALFOUR said he had come to the conclusion that if the Committee would be content to fix a limit of 20,0 E population in the non- county boroughs which should have educational authori- ties the Government would be prepared to risk the ex- periment. Mr. GODSON moved,. as an amendment to the original amendment, to add the words and not less than 20,000 inhabitants," and this was carried by 287 votes to 117. A division on Sir A. Rollit's amendment as amended resulted in its adoption by 332 votes to 83.

div.head: ST. BARNABAS CIIU-RVH, WARRINGTON.
div.p: ST. BARNABAS CIIU-RVH, WARRINGTON.
BAZAAR AT THIO CONSERVATIVE CLUB.

On Wednesday afternooa a bazaar was opener' in. the Assembly room of the Conservative Club, Warrington,to assist the effrt which is being made to provide a stipend for:the support of a curate in the parish of St. Barnabas. Mr. R. Pierpoint M.P., opened the bazaar, in the pres- ence of a very meagre attendance. Before the ceremony, the vicar, the Rev. G. ALLTON said they had not had a bazaar, in connection with their parish since 1885. From the formation of the parish they had wanted pretty nearly everything except a church, which was-already built. They had since erected two schools and a good vicarage house. Persons wth money and influence were required to make a place prosperous and them were very few in the parish. Et curate was required and a sale. I of work was the only .neans of starting a stipend to- wards installing one. For five years they had waited, and now they were trying to get up a fund to pay a curate and also to provide for much-needed repairs to the church. Notable among the contributors were those few old friends who had supported the church from the commencement :—Lord Lilford,. Lady Greenall, Mrs. Lyon, Mr. Robert Pierpoint, Miss Pierpoint and others. Mr. R. PIERPOINT, M.P., said it gave him great plea sure to officiate at the opening of that sale of work. The 'needs of the parish had been eloquently spoken of by Mr. Allton who had reminded them that the parish was one that suffered from the fact that it had practically no people of wealth in it. It therefore depended greatly for encouragement and help from people of mean, out- side. To the names Mr. Allton had mentioned he thought they ought to add Lord Winmarleigh. (Ap- plause.) It was a pleasure to the speaker to have to tell them that he the previous night received a letter from Lady Greenall in which she promised a donation ok £2O to- wards the amount which they were trying to raise. (Applause.) Mr. Pierpoint then declared the bazaar open. Mr.Towmas proposed a vote of thanks to Mr.Pierpoint for his attendance. The Rev. G. ALLTON seconded, and said he hoped Mr. Pierpoint would , convey their hearty thanks to Lady Greenall. Mr. PIERPOINT, before going, added £5 to the list of donations. _

There were seven stalls in the room containing the usual misGellanea of fancy goods, drapery, and they were presided over as follows :—Sundav school stall, Miss Helsby, Miss Evans, and Miss Wilson ; Vicarage stall, Mrs. Allton and Mrs. Jones; Vicar's stall, thd Rev. G. Allton and Miss A. Allton ; Churchwarden's stall, Mrs. Looker. Mrs. Trevitt, and Mrs. Edwardson ; Children's stall. Miss Amy Allton ; Refreshment stall, Mrs. Bellian, Mrs. Randall, and Mrs. Smith ; Mothers' Class stall, Mrs. Potter. The sale was continued during the evening, and alto- gether realised £

A REVOLUTION IN THE WEAVING TRADE.—i party of capitalists and experts met on Tuesday at the works of Messrs. Turner and Co., at Cononley, near Bradford, to view the working of the new "double pick shuttle." Messrs. D'Andria and Slicer's Pnvention is simple, con- sisting as it does of a shuttle of ordinary length, but broader than that now used ,and so arranged as to carry two bobbins of weft. The result of this is that as the shuttle passes through the warp-shed the weft threads are laid in such a manner that the reeds beat them up to the cloth parallel to each other and there is no risk of one overriding the other, thus ensuring evenness of tex- ture. From the demonstrations given, any loom can be easily converted at a small cost to the "double pick,"by the mere addition of a wider " race." At the same time it must be remembered that the wide race is equally adaptable to the ordinary shuttle. The looms can be run at the ordinary rate of speed, and at the same time turn out twice the amount of material. The fact that several looms are and have been for some time in work with eminently satisfactory results,is good proof of the value of the invention.

CRICKET.

Perhaps never in the history of the Sefton Club hw Warrington inflicted such a crushing defeat as that which they administered on the Sefton Park ground on Saturday. To win by the handsome majority of 143 runs,.nd at Sefton too,is a performance which the War- rington team may well be proud of. The result was quite as much a surprise to many in Warrington as it. would be to Seftonians,for the Warrington team was not one of the best elevens that has represented the " good old town "this season. Mr. S. M. Crosfield, we under- stand,has departed for Iceland, and it will be some time before he again figures in the Warrington team. Another absentee on Saturday was Mr. J. J. Crosfield, but Mr. G. Crosfield proved a good substitute, and for the first time this season, Mr. G. Clarke made his, ap- pearance in the teatn,and assumed the role of captain,a position which he filled with credit.

Winning the toss, Mr. Clarke decided that his team should be the first to go to the wickets. The Sefton team were a man short at the commencement, and Mr. Clarke fielded as a substitute until the arrival of Brock. It was whilst acting in this capacity, that Mr. Clarke by a brilliant catch at cover point, had the somewhat un- pleasant experience of getting one of his own mem out in the person of Thewlis. The start was anytbirg but promising for the visitors. Thewlis, Podin9re and Cal- lon were all out before the score had reached 24. On Connor and England becoming associated, a different complexion was placed upon the game. Connor, in his usual vigorous manner severely punished the bowl.;^ig of Marshall, and it was not until he had compiled 29 :Tins, that he was caught and bowled by Stewart, who bad had the satisfaction of taking all the previous wichets. England continued to play cautiously. but Clarke his new partner, soon sent the ball rolling to the boundary. This performance he repeated in quick succession, and made 27 in a short time. England felt to a catch by Lacey when he had scored 17.

But the stand of the afternoon was yet to be made, for wheta Bibby and. Hampson became partners some splendid batting was seen. Both played cautiously until they had become familiar with the bowling, and then they warmed to their work. Hampson struck out with vigour, placing ball after ball to the boundary. Bibby followed suit, but Hampson scored the faster of the two. Several changes of bowling were tried with- out effect, and the 200 was hoisted amid cheers. At 209, however, a fine catch on the boundary,dismissed Hamp- son who had played fine cricket for his 71 runs. There seems to be a peculiar charm about the figures." 71" for Warrington cricketers, for net only has it been. exactly reached three times this season, but 71 is also the high- est individual score which has been made by a member of the Warrington team this year. The three* players who have now reached that figure are S. M. Crosfield, Thewlis and Mampson. Hampson's contribution on Saturday included no fewer than twelve fours.. The match was only proceeded with until his cc-partner (Bibby) had compiled 50. This he accomplished succes- fully, and the Warrington innings was then declared closed, the score being 211 for 8 wickets. On retiring to the pavilion, Bibby was loudly applauded, his excellent innings of 50 not out, including nine fours. His per- formance should materially assist his average.

Sefton commenced their innings with C. L. Jones acrid Tongue, but before anything had been scored, Jones had the misfortune to have his finger hurt by a ball from Scrimshaw. Armstrong succeeded him, and before long Connor sent him back to the pavilion by sending him down a slow ball which he struck at before it had tra- velled half-way down the pitch. Scrimshaw, however, carried oi the palm of the bowling honours, taking seven wickets for 26 runs. Only three of the Sefton men teached double figures, and the whole team was dig. missed for 66 runs. The bowlers were well backed up in their efforts by spltndid fielding, and fine catches were made by England, Podmore, and Crosfield. The latter was successful with two catches, and was very smart in the field.

Another match was played on Monday afternoon at Old Trafford, when Warrinkton engaged the Manchester eleven. The visiting team was by no means strong, several reserves having to be requisitioned. Connor was among the absentees and his skill in bowling was greatly required towards theend of the game.Warrington batted first and were all dismissed for the small total of 121. This did not give the Mancurians an arduous task, and it is scarcely doubtful that they would have won hand- somely but for the unlooked for advent of a thunder- storm, which put a stop to hostilities with the home score standing just S short of the visitors' for S wickets down. k draw, lucky for Warrington, was the result.

The match was an interesting one so far as it went, and some good play was witnessed. W.R.Podrnore and Thewlis initiated the Warrington innings, but only a couple of runs had been made by the latter when Pod- more placed the ball into the hands of the man at cover slip. Callon jcined the Warrington pro. ,and played with great caution. Thewlis scored the majority of runs, Huddleston and Wright being driven to the boundary several times by him. Callon was shortly dismissed fr,r 15, and G. Clarke had hardly got going before C.H.Ben- ton forced him to concedo a "catch." Thewlis next re- tired from the same cause after having compiled a use- ful and stylish 26: A.C.Ndson and G.Hampson entered into partnership, but when the score of the former stood for 3iruns, he was.caught by Fullalove. M.Silcock next joined Hampson, and a long stand was the result. Hampson defended well, and Siicock hit out cqually well,, so that a total. of 87 was reached be- fore the Warrington wicket-keeper slipped the ball into Pope's hands. E. Nelson and Linney both joined Silcock but were unable to do anything against the bowling. Silcock eventually missed a full-pitched ball from Huddlestoa, and retired with a well hit 37 to his credit. The last two of the visiting eleven, Scrimshaw and G. Crosfield, also made a good stand and increased 1.1-- --ore by 311 runs before the professional was bowled for 20.

Though the task for the home team was by no means an ardueus one, yet the first five wickets were down for only 45 runs. Thewlis and Scrimshaw being the success- ful bowlers. The Warrington barometer rose high, but needlessly, Thr C. Hartley and G. Radcliffe almost settled the match by the fine partnership they formed. Only &runs were required to see the visitors sent home defeated when a thunderstorm compelled the batsmen to retire. neither being out. Hartley had scored 48 and Radcliffe 2Clincreasing the total for their side to 113. A wait of nearly an hour was made but the storm was determined in its persistence and the game had to be declared drawn.

The prowess of the second eleven was further preyed on Saturday when they beat the Sefton " A" team by 61. runs. Speculation before the match was, of course, rife, and it was not uncommonly thought that the home team would have considerable difficulty in emerging victors from the fray. The Sefton club was credited with having some good batsmen and their chances were consideted favourable. The Warrington innings realised 143 runs and this was not looked upon as a safe figure but the results proved it to have been more than was required'.

Siitock and Adamson set the ball rolling for the home innings and scoring immediately began to mount up, but after Silceck had hit Brotherton pretty freely about the field a long pitched one beat him and he retired with a round dozen to his name. Adamson remained in and made the stand of the match,4/ being his total when the umnire gave him out. Rushworth and Cooke proved good partners also, the former compiling 26 and the latter 22. Smith was not out for la. The innings of A‘hton and Lowe caused some amusement. Ashton on reaching the crease prepared himself for negotiating the boundary,and his first ball being a very tempting one,he " let out "at it, but alas, the leather was a little too quick for the batsmen and " spread" the stomps. Lowe did a trifle better, inasmuch as he outlived half an over before being clean bowled.

Boqwell and Ratcliffe started for Sefton, but Silcock's first ball dismissed the former player. Following this, the Sefton men did little against the bowling, Marrow making the top score with 18. Fielding was smart on the Warrington side and Sefton were all out for 82. War- rin.ton people had evidently a little too exalted an idea of the skill of the Sefton Parkites.

The Sankey Bridges Wesleyan C.C. opened their new ground on Saturday by a match with the Windsor Wes- leyan C.C. (Liverpool). There was a numerous attend- ance of spectators. The Liverpool team batted first but could only make 44 runs against the bowling of Llewellyn and Watkins. The home team scored 91 runs, their best batsmen being F. Taylor, Llewllyn, and Sad- low. By this victory the greund has been auspiciously opened and it is naturally the desire of all the club's surporters, that many more successes may be witnessed on the field which the generosity of Mr. W. Brough has provided.

Messrs. P. Walker and Son's team continued on their career of success on Saturday, when they wiped out the Lostock Gralam eleven to the tune of 120 against 43. Of the visitors' total 18 was compiled by Billington, the only player of his side to reach double figures. The brewery team did not commence in a much more prom- ising manner for there were three wickets down for 15 runs. Ashton was, however, piling up the runs and in fact decided the match before being out, with a score of 56 runs. Todd added 21 to this total and Milner carried out his bat for 11. The winners are becoming known as one of the best of the local teams.

Mercer Street Stanley Street Walmsley Street Haydock Street Blrley Street Peel Street Water Street Alpine streot Bradlegh Road Back Market Street NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the Urban Distect Council of Newton-in-Makerfield being the Urban Sanitary Authority for the said District at a meeting duly convened and held on the Ist day of June, 1896. Be- - solved, that we do hereby approve of the specifications, plans and sections, an estimate of the probable expenses of the works together with a provisional apportionment of the esti- mated expenses among the premises liable to be charged therewith in respect of the aforesaid Streets, now submitted by the Surveyor, and we do hereby order and direct by this resolution, tbatthe aforesail Streets, or parts of such Streets, shall be sewered, levelled, paved,metalled, flagged.channelled and otherwise made good to the satistaction of this Council, pursuant to the provisions of the Private Street Works Act, 1892. The said specifications, plans and sections, estimates, and provisional apportionments (or duly certified copies thereof) will be depcsited during one month from the Fifth day of June, 1896, at the office of the Surveyor to the Council,at the Town Hall, Earlestown, and will be open to inspection at all reasonable times. COUNTY OF CHESTER, TO WIT. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER will be holden at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 29th day of June next, at half-past eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hun- dreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all pri- soners committed from such Hundreds will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 29th day of June next, at half-past eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. The COURT will be Adjourned to the Court House. Knutsford, on WEDNESDAY, the Ist day of July next, at eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on WEDNESDAY, the Ist day of July next, at eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS. Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester, Chester, Bth June, 1896.
